column3:
Market liberalisation level
Format: Sentence stating retail/wholesale competition + presence of dominant incumbents.
Example: “Fully liberalised retail and wholesale markets; incumbent state?owned supplier remains dominant.”
column4:
Renewable energy production
Format: 1 sentence summarising RES share and key technologies (no exact % needed).
Example: “High RES share with strong wind and hydro; solar growing rapidly.”
column5:
Grid structure
Format: 2–3 phrases on TSO/DSO ownership and DSO landscape (single vs many DSOs).
Example: “Single national TSO; one large national DSO plus local municipal DSOs.”
column6:
Number of energy communities
Format: Latest national estimate + year + source tag (short).
Example: “?700 registered ECs (2023, national report).”
column7:
Number of identified cVPPs
Format: Integer or “none identified / pilots only”, plus very short clarification if needed.
Example: “No explicit cVPP pilots identified; only ECs using CSC model.
column8:
Technologies of energy communities
Format: 1–2 sentences listing dominant technologies and any notable patterns (e.g. hydro, rooftop PV, onshore wind).
Example: “ECs mainly develop rooftop PV and onshore wind; some small hydro projects.”
column10:
Notes
Format: Max 2–3 sentences with any contextual nuance about the EC/cVPP landscape that doesn’t fit above (e.g. strong national network, political targets).
column11:
REC Legal status
Format: “Yes/No + where/how defined + very short qualifier (primary law vs scheme).”
Example: “Yes – defined in Renewable Energy Act and Electricity Law as specific legal entity.”
column12:
CEC Legal status
Format: Same as REC but for CEC; if merged into a single EC category, say so.
Example: “No separate CEC; electricity?market directive transposed via a unified ‘energy community’ definition.”
column13:
Transposition Completeness
Format: “Complete / Partial / Not transposed + 1 clause on missing element if any.”
Example: “Complete – REC/CEC provisions integrated in Energy Code; no CEC?specific registry.”
column14:
Specific legal rights
Format: 1–2 sentences listing what ECs are explicitly allowed to do (generate, share, supply, aggregate, own networks, provide services).
Example: “ECs may generate, consume, store, share and sell electricity, participate in all markets directly or via aggregators; cannot own public electricity networks.”
column15:
Dedicated energy communities framework
Format: “Yes/No + main instruments (acts, codes, decrees).”
Example: “Yes – dedicated EC title in Energy Code plus implementing decree on energy communities.”
column16:
Administrative/Bureaucratic complexity
Format: 1–2 sentences on registration/notification, licensing, ability to form ECs administratively.
Example: “No separate EC registry; ECs must notify DSOs and comply with standard project permitting; supply?licence exemptions limited to specific EC conditions.”
column18:
Notes
Format: 1–2 sentences capturing structural peculiarities (e.g. overlapping pre?existing frameworks, ongoing reforms).
column19:
Allowed legal forms
Format: List of main legal forms that ECs may take (co?op, association, company, etc.).
Example: “Cooperatives, associations, limited companies and municipalities’ SEM?type entities.”
column20:
Equity ownership
Format: 1–2 sentences on who can be members/owners + non?profit or profit caps + any caps on shareholding.
Example: “Members can be citizens, SMEs and local authorities; primary purpose must be non?profit; individual shareholding capped at 25% of voting rights.”
column21:
Geographic/spatial constraints
Format: 1 sentence on proximity rules for members/control (if any).
Example: “REC control must be exercised by members located in the same or adjacent municipality; no proximity requirement for CECs.”
column22:
Citizen participation
Format: 1–2 sentences describing forms/extent of citizen membership and voting rights.
Example: “Open and voluntary participation; citizen or local?authority member category must hold effective control (>40% of votes).”
column23:
Role of public actors
Format: 1–2 sentences on municipalities/regions/state roles as members, investors, organisers.
Example: “Local authorities can join and co?own projects; some ECs are initiated or majority?owned by municipalities.”
column24:
Role/participation of third party
Format: 1–2 sentences on involvement of commercial developers, suppliers, crowdfunding platforms, etc.
Example: “Commercial RES developers may co?own projects; crowdfunding platforms and social?impact funds participate as minority investors.”
column26:
notes
Format: Short nuance on typical governance configurations (e.g. “citizen?majority co?ops dominate”, “many mixed public?private vehicles”).
column27:
Energy sharing permitted? and how?
Format: “Yes/No + short description of legal mechanism (CSC, peer?to?peer, etc.).”
Example: “Yes – via collective self?consumption scheme where EC legal entity allocates shared production among members.”
column28:
Model type
Format: 1 sentence naming the main operational model (CSC, local tariff, pure generation?only, etc.).
Example: “Collective self?consumption of local PV with residual supply from commercial supplier.”
column29:
Geographical boundaries/scope
Format: 1 sentence describing allowed perimeter (building, LV feeder, km radius, DSO area, etc.).
Example: “Default building?level; can extend to 2 km (LV, ?3 MW) and exceptionally to 20 km by ministerial exemption.”
column30:
Supplier intermediation
Format: 1 sentence on whether a supplier is required and how (same supplier for all, any supplier, EC as supplier, etc.).
Example: “Participants keep individual supply contracts; same supplier must support energy sharing for all participating members.”
column31:
Regulatory complexity/bottleneck
Format: 1–2 sentences on key constraints that complicate energy sharing (licence requirements, meter rules, perimeter caps).
Example: “Energy sharing only via CSC; strict meter and perimeter rules; complex choice of sharing rules subject to DSO validation.”
column33:
Notes
Format: Any nuance on sharing?rule options, default rules, observed practice (e.g. “most use default pro?rata to consumption rule”).
column34:
Smart meter roll out
Format: short indicator + brief description.
Example: “?90% rollout (2024); advanced meters mandatory for CSC/energy?sharing participants.”
column35:
Data granularity
Format: smallest time step used for billing/allocation (15?min, 30?min, hourly).
Example: “15?minute data aligned with balancing period.”
column36:
Data access rights
Format: 1–2 sentences on who can access meter data (EC, supplier, DSO, member) and under what conditions.
Example: “DSO collects and shares quarter?hourly data with suppliers; EC or legal entity receives allocation data; members can access own data via portal.”
column38:
Notes
Format: Short mention of key barriers (e.g. incomplete rollout, lack of standard substitute?value procedures).
column39:
Aggregation allowed
Format: “Yes/No + scope (generation, demand response, both).”
Example: “Yes – ECs can aggregate generation and demand?response resources.”
column40:
Independent aggregation
Format: 1 sentence on whether independent aggregators (separate from suppliers) are recognised and allowed.
Example: “Independent aggregators recognised in law; ECs can contract with them or become aggregators under general rules.”
column41:
Community aggregators role
Format: 1–2 sentences describing whether ECs themselves can act as aggregators and under what conditions.
Example: “CEC framework allows ECs to provide aggregation services; no separate ‘community aggregator’ licence.”
column43:
Notes
Format: Any nuance on interaction with DSOs/TSOs or balancing market access.
column44:
Market Access
Access type
Format: 1–2 sentences summarising which markets ECs can enter (retail supply, wholesale, balancing, capacity, local flexibility).
Example: “ECs can sell into wholesale markets via suppliers/aggregators and participate in national support schemes; no dedicated local flexibility market yet.”
column45:
Wholesale
Format: 1 sentence on whether ECs can directly trade in wholesale markets or must go through intermediaries.
Example: “Direct wholesale participation is possible but uncommon; most ECs rely on PPAs with suppliers.”
column46:
Main actors
Format: key institutional players relevant to EC market access (regulator, TSO/DSO, main programmes).
Example: “Energy regulator, TSO, national DSO and community?support organisations (e.g. REScoop, Energie Partagée).”
column48:
Notes
Format: brief note on any specific EC?related market rule (e.g. priority access, non?discrimination clauses).
column49:
Pricing
Network charges
Format: 1 sentence on whether shared/self?consumed energy pays full network tariffs, reduced ones, or exemptions.
Example: “Shared energy pays full volumetric grid tariffs; no specific EC reduction.”
column50:
DSO / distribution pricing
Format: 1 sentence on DSO tariff structure relevant to ECs (capacity vs energy?based, differentiation by voltage level).
Example: “Two?part tariff (capacity + energy) with reduced energy charge for local REC energy flows.”
column51:
Financial support schemes
Format: 1–2 sentences naming key schemes relevant to ECs (FiT, premiums, grants, tenders, bonuses) and whether any are EC?specific.
Example: “RES tenders with bonus points for citizen/local authority ownership; feed?in premium for small citizen wind projects; grants for community heating networks.
column53:
Notes
Format: nuance on how pricing and support interact with EC viability (e.g. recent reforms that hurt small projects).
column54:
Energy Justice
Procedural justice
Format: 1–2 sentences describing who can form/operate ECs, how accessible procedures are, and whether rights are explicit.
Example: “Any citizen, SME or local authority can form ECs; procedures complex but rights are clearly stated in Energy Code; no one?stop national registry.”
column55:
Distributive justice
Format: 1–2 sentences on how risks/costs/benefits are shared (e.g. who bears balancing risk, who benefits from CBFs or tariffs).
Example: “Members bear part of revenue risk (market?linked income); some schemes channel benefits via community funds and tariff bonuses.”
column59:
Legal barriers
Format: bullet?like phrase listing 1–2 key legal obstacles.
Example: “Ambiguous profit thresholds; exclusion of certain non?profits from EC membership.”
column60:
Market barriers
Format: 1–2 key market design issues.
Example: “No clear route for ECs to monetise flexibility; complex PPA requirements.”
column61:
Technical barriers
Format: 1–2 key technical issues.
Example: “Incomplete smart?meter coverage; complex metering for multi?EC participants.”
column62:
Economic barriers
Format: 1–2 key financial issues.
Example: “Small projects struggle to access bank finance; support schemes favour larger developers.”
column63:
Social barriers
Format: 1–2 key socio?political issues.
Example: “Low awareness in low?income communities; limited time/capacity among volunteers.”
column64:
Other barriers
Format: anything not fitting above (e.g. environmental siting conflicts, defence?area restrictions).
column65:
Opportunities
Format: 1–2 sentences on main enabling opportunities (policy reforms, support networks, targets).

column2: Hydro?dominated, highly renewable electricity system with strong public and municipal actors
column3: Formally liberalised wholesale and retail markets since the 2000s, with regulated network monopolies and a mix of public and private suppliers and DSOs
column4: Around three?quarters of electricity generation from renewables, with hydropower providing over 60% and growing wind, solar and biomass shares
column5: Single national TSO (APG) operating the high?voltage backbone grid and multiple regional DSOs managing distribution networks, including municipal and utility?owned distributors
column6: Several hundred RECs and CECs registered or listed in the national CEOC registry, which is voluntary and does not capture all existing ECs
column7: No explicitly branded cVPP pilots identified; EC activity is mainly via REC/CEC energy?sharing configurations
column8: ECs are primarily based on rooftop and ground?mounted PV, often combined with small?scale storage and, in some cases, small hydro, biomass or wind installations
column10: Austria combines a very high renewable share and a hydro?dominated system with an advanced legal framework for RECs and CECs; the COEC registry and evaluation report show a fast?growing but heterogeneous EC landscape, where most initiatives are small PV?based projects embedded in local or regional grids and supported by reduced grid tariffs for RECs.
column11: Yes - REC defined in the Renewable Energy Expansion Act (EAG) + Renewable Energy Expansion Acceleration Act (2025) and the Electricity Industry and Organisation Act (EIWOG) as a legal entity with at least two members that enables sharing of renewable energy within the community; framework introduced through the 2021 EAG package
column12: Yes - CEC defined in EIWOG Section 6a ff. as a legal entity controlled by its members or shareholders (natural or legal persons and local authorities), with open and voluntary participation and a primary non?profit purpose; distinct from the REC definition and not mentioned in the EAG
column13: Complete – REC and CEC concepts are fully transposed via EAG (for RECs) and EIWOG (for CECs), including detailed rights, obligations, energy?sharing rules and enabling provisions
column14: Network users have a legal right vis?à?vis network operators to participate in a REC or CEC without losing free supplier choice; RECs and CECs may generate, consume, store and sell self?generated electricity, and RECs may share self?generated renewable electricity among members; operation and maintenance can be delegated to third parties
column15: Yes – comprehensive EC framework through EAG Section 6 (RECs) and EIWOG Section 6a ff. (CECs), with common energy?sharing provisions, supported institutionally by the federal Coordination Office for Energy Communities (COEC).
column16: Straightforward notification?based procedure but with detailed information requirements: ECs must notify the DSO/network operator of plant characteristics, meters, planned production and consumption shares, and 15?minute allocation of non?consumed energy; since April 2024 generation plants and consumers can participate in multiple RECs/CECs, which complicates billing, contracts and customer information.

column18: REC and CEC activities are exempt from the 1994 Industrial Code and thus are not treated as regulated commercial trades, but the December 2024 evaluation highlights multiple legal ambiguities (profit thresholds, market?premium rules, storage treatment) and calls for clarifications in forthcoming ElWG and EABG legislation.
column19: RECs and CECs must be organised as an association, cooperative, partnership, corporation or similar association with legal personality.
column20: REC members and shareholders can be natural persons, municipalities, specific public?law entities and SMEs; energy suppliers cannot participate and REC participation must not be a main commercial or professional activity; CEC members can be natural or legal persons and local authorities, but control must rest with one or more of the following: natural persons, local authorities, or small enterprises that are not electricity companies.
column21: REC members and shareholders must be located in the vicinity of the production site; energy sharing is restricted to the low?voltage grid plus the low?voltage part of the transformer (local area) or the medium?voltage network plus the MV point in the substation (regional area) within the DSO concession; energy transmission for REC sharing cannot exceed the MV substation level; CECs have no explicit geographical proximity requirement
column22: Participation in RECs and CECs must be open and voluntary, and both types must have a primary purpose of delivering environmental, economic or social benefits rather than financial profit; in CECs, effective control must be held by natural persons, local authorities or small non?electricity enterprises, while REC statutes must ensure that energy suppliers do not control the entity.
column23: Municipalities, other public?law entities and local authorities may be members of both RECs and CECs and, for CECs, can hold control; the Federal Ministry for Climate Action and the regulator E?Control oversee the framework and evaluations, while the national Coordination Office for Energy Communities and federal?state coordination hubs (e.g. UIV, Energieagentur Tirol) support implementation.
column24: RECs and CECs may delegate operation and maintenance of plants to third parties and must cooperate with licensed DSOs/network operators for metering and allocation; energy suppliers may not be REC members, but producers injecting into local or regional networks and service providers can participate under the general rules
column26: COEC and state?level agencies function as governance intermediaries, providing information, templates and guidance to municipalities and citizen groups, while the December 2024 evaluation stresses that unclear profit thresholds and the exclusion of many welfare and non?profit organisations (treated as large companies) from REC participation create equity concerns.
column27: Yes – energy sharing is central to the REC/CEC frameworks; for RECs the main activity is sharing self?generated renewable electricity among members, and both RECs and CECs are covered by common energy?sharing provisions on measurement, allocation, billing and data access
column28: REC: locality?based collective self?consumption and sharing of renewable generation within defined local or regional grid areas; CEC: broader electricity community that can generate, consume, store and sell electricity and be active in aggregation and other energy services across all voltage levels
column29: REC energy sharing is restricted to the LV network plus the LV part of the transformer (local) or the MV network plus the MV point in the substation (regional) within the DSO concession area; energy transmission for shared REC energy cannot exceed the MV substation; CECs have no explicit geographical proximity requirement and may operate at all voltage levels
column30: DSOs measure and allocate quarter?hourly energy flows for EC participants; suppliers receive only the data relevant to their activity and bill residual consumption, while the REC/CEC or an appointed third party bills the shared energy to members according to the agreed remuneration model, which can include a zero price.
column31: REC and CEC establishment requires detailed notification to DSOs (plants, meters, planned shares, 15?minute allocation of non?consumed energy), and since April 2024 both generation systems and consumers can belong to multiple ECs, which complicates allocation, billing and electricity bills; lack of smart?meter data and non?standardised substitute?value processes further delays energy allocation and settlements.
column33: The law requires 15?minute metering for energy sharing, with measured values reduced by the allocated generated energy for balancing; quarter?hourly values must be made available by the next day free of charge via a secure web portal, and DSOs must also transmit data to the regulator for compliance checks and the annual EC report.
column34: Smart?meter roll?out is incomplete (29%, JRC 2022) but mandatory for EC participants; if a network user wishing to join a REC/CEC does not have a smart meter, the DSO must install one within two months.
column35: For energy sharing, metering and allocation are performed every 15 minutes, and quarter?hourly generation and consumption values must be provided to suppliers and the REC/CEC by the following day.
column36: REC/CEC and their members must receive quarter?hourly metering and allocation data free of charge via a safe, user?friendly, encrypted web portal; DSOs must also provide relevant data to the regulator for random and ad hoc checks and for the annual EC report
column38: Current lack of smart?meter coverage and non?harmonised substitute?value processes across DSOs delays allocation and billing, and the December 2024 evaluation recommends clear legal requirements for a uniform substitute?value process to improve EC data handling.
column39: Yes - RECs can be active in aggregation and provide other energy services, and CECs may generate, consume, store and sell electricity and be active in aggregation and energy services for their members.
column40: Aggregators must cooperate with licensed DSOs, and there is no explicit regime for independent aggregators within the EC framework; in principle ECs could act as aggregators, but this is not explicitly regulated as a separate category.
column41: RECs and CECs may aggregate their members’ generation and consumption and provide services such as flexibility or efficiency, but they must comply with general market and DSO rules, and their contribution to system costs and balancing is monitored through a cost?benefit analysis.
column43: Grid operators and suppliers retain formal responsibility for balancing and forecasting in most setups, while the regulator’s cost?benefit analysis concluded that, at current levels, RECs/CECs have no significant effect on overall grid tariffs but do impose connection?investment costs on DSOs
column44: Network users have a legal right to participate in RECs/CECs without losing free supplier choice; ECs may sell surplus electricity into the public grid and access support schemes (investment grants and market premiums) under national RES rules.
column45: ECs typically sell surplus electricity into the public grid and may receive market premiums via tenders; balancing and forecasting are handled by grid operators and suppliers, while ECs’ system?cost contributions, including balancing, are monitored by the regulator.
column46: Federal Ministry for Climate Action, Environment, Energy, Mobility, Innovation and Technology; E?Control (regulator); DSOs and TSOs; the Coordination Office for Energy Communities (COEC) and its regional?level coordination hubs.
column49: For REC members, the fixed (capacity?based) portion of the grid fee is reduced in line with lower power drawn from the public grid, and the energy?price (volume?based) part of the grid?use charge on shared energy is reduced according to geography: 57% if the REC operates only at local level; 28% at local level or 64% at regional level for RECs operating both local and regional; these reductions must be shown explicitly on bills in EUR cents/kWh.
column50: For REC members, network?usage fees are calculated separately based on consumption covered by allocated shared energy, with reductions in both capacity? and energy?based components; CECs do not benefit from specific grid?charge reductions because they are not subject to a proximity requirement and may use higher?level networks
column51: From 2023, market premiums are awarded solely through competitive tenders, with tendering requirements applying only partly to wind plants under 20 MW and those operated by RECs/CECs; up to 50% of renewable electricity generated and not consumed within a REC/CEC can receive a market premium based on electricity sold into the public grid, while energy shared and consumed within ECs is not premium?eligible and not counted when determining the renewable levy for consumers; RECs and CECs are also eligible for investment grants (e.g. for PV, storage, hydro, wind, biomass), and the government has committed dedicated funding for establishing ECs
column53: The December 2024 evaluation flags ambiguities around market?premium rules and their interaction with EC sharing, which can create uncertainty for long?term offtake and external financing of EC plants
column54:

Draft provisions for RECs require explicit elements in funding documents regarding member rights
column55:
Reduced grid tariffs for REC members and exemptions from the renewable levy for shared energy make EC participation financially attractive, but unclear profit?orientation thresholds and rules on surplus use create uncertainty about how benefits can be distributed, and the proximity criterion can limit socially defined communities that span multiple grid areas.

column59: Official evaluation identifies unclear non?profit/profit thresholds, ambiguous market?premium rules, lack of clear storage?integration rules, and exclusion of many welfare and non?profit organisations (classified as large companies) from REC participation as significant legal barriers
column60: Competitive tenders combined with capped and partly ambiguous premiums expose ECs to higher revenue uncertainty and make project financing more difficult; there is also a risk of market discrimination if cost?allocation and balancing rules are not adjusted as EC numbers grow.
column61: Insufficient smart?meter deployment and non?standardised substitute?value processes hinder timely allocation and billing; multi?EC participation and the use of one plant for multiple ECs increase technical and contractual complexity, and the absence of clear storage rules limits the development of more advanced EC configurations
column62: Revenue uncertainty linked to tender?based premiums and unclear surplus?distribution rules, together with the exclusion of many large non?profit organisations from REC membership, constrain capital mobilisation and limit the ability to use ECs for social?sector decarbonisation
column63: Inadequate inclusion of vulnerable households, limited social?tariff models in ECs and the exclusion of many welfare organisations from REC membership mean that low?income and vulnerable groups do not yet benefit proportionately from EC schemes.
column64: Complex billing structures for members participating in multiple ECs and non?standardised contracts for community plants increase transaction costs for both citizens and suppliers
column65: Strong national one?stop?shop (COEC), clear REC/CEC legal frameworks, reduced grid tariffs for RECs and planned legislation (ElWG, EABG) to simplify approvals and support small?scale energy exchange create a solid foundation; the 2024 evaluation suggests targeted reforms (profit thresholds, storage rules, vulnerable?household inclusion, broader REC eligibility) to enhance justice and scalability of ECs.

column2: Centralised, nuclear?anchored system with growing gas and renewables; transmission and large?scale generation are federal competences, while regions control distribution, retail regulation and most renewables
column3: Fully liberalised wholesale and retail electricity markets with multiple suppliers and DSOs; historical incumbents (notably ENGIE Electrabel and regionally dominant DSOs/suppliers) still hold significant market shares despite formal unbundling.
column4: Moderate but increasing RES share, with onshore wind and solar PV as the main growth vectors; hydro is limited and biomass plays a secondary role, with regional targets and support schemes driving additional PV and wind deployment.
column5: Single national TSO (Elia) responsible for transmission, system operation and offshore integration at federal level, combined with a fragmented DSO landscape where multiple regional and municipal DSOs operate low? and medium?voltage networks under Flemish, Walloon and Brussels?Capital regulation.
column6: Several hundred initiatives across Belgium, with dozens of formally registered or emerging RECs/CECs per region and a larger ecosystem of legacy energy cooperatives; recent regional fiches point to a rapidly growing pipeline rather than a fully stabilised national registry.
column7: No explicit, large?scale cVPPs identified in official registries; instead, there are EC?type pilots with advanced management and flexibility features in Flanders and some regional smart?grid and flexibility projects that could evolve toward cVPP configurations
column8: Belgian ECs are predominantly centred on rooftop and small?scale PV, often combined with collective self?consumption and local sharing; there is additional activity around onshore wind cooperatives and early experiments with storage, EV charging and flexibility services, especially in Flanders and Brussels.
column10: The division of competences between federal and regional levels produces three distinct regional EC frameworks layered on a shared federal market structure, which is analytically useful for understanding how tariff design, data access and energy?sharing rules shape EC and cVPP prospects within one country. The strong tradition of citizen energy cooperatives provides organisational capacity and capital for ECs, but the complexity of multi?level regulation and DSO fragmentation can raise transaction costs and complicate the emergence of fully fledged cVPPs
column11: Yes – REC is defined in federal primary law (Law of 23 October 2022 amending the Act of 29 April 1999 on the electricity market) and in regional primary/secondary legislation in Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels (energy/market decrees and ordinances), as an autonomous legal entity with open and voluntary participation, effective local control and a primary environmental, economic or social benefit purpose.
column12: Yes – CEC is likewise defined in the same federal law and in regional electricity/energy acts (Flemish Energy Decree, Walloon Decree of 5 May 2022, Brussels Ordinance of 20 April 2022) as a specific legal entity; RECs and CECs are both recognised, and “energy community” is generally used as an umbrella term that includes both rather than merging them into a single undifferentiated category
column13: Partial to advanced – REC and CEC definitions and basic rights have been transposed at federal and regional levels, including energy?sharing possibilities and an enabling framework, but several Clean Energy Package elements remain incomplete or uneven (for example, fully harmonised simplified licensing, balance?responsibility arrangements and EC?specific tariff rules are still being developed and differ between regions)
column14: RECs and CECs may produce, self?consume, store and share energy, provide or participate in energy services, act as flexibility or aggregation providers, sell electricity (including under PPAs) and offer EV?charging services, with financial responsibility for imbalances that can be delegated to a balancing?responsible party. They have a right to cost?reflective, non?discriminatory network tariffs and protection against disproportionate technical, administrative and licensing requirements, although in practice many market?facing activities still require cooperation with licensed suppliers or aggregator
column15: Yes – there is a dedicated EC framework spread across the federal electricity?market act (as amended by the Law of 23 October 2022) and regional instruments: the Flemish Energy Decree and implementing decisions, the Walloon Decree of 5 May 2022 plus the Government decision of 17 March 2023, and the Brussels?Capital Ordinance of 20 April 2022 on the organisation of the electricity and gas markets.
column16: ECs must adopt a general legal form under company or association law and include detailed EC?specific clauses in their statutes (control, proximity, objectives, profit use, entry/exit rules), then register or be authorised with the relevant regional regulator (e.g. Brugel in Brussels, CREG/CWaPE/VREG frameworks) and act as a single point of contact for the DSO. They face region?specific notification, metering and data?exchange procedures, and while the law prohibits disproportionate requirements, the multiplicity of regional rules, statutory content conditions and ongoing balance?responsibility and licensing obligations creates a relatively high administrative burden, especially for small citizen groups
column18: Belgium’s EC framework is explicitly multi?level: federal law embeds REC/CEC concepts and some rights (especially around tariffs, flexibility and offshore participation), while concrete implementation, registries and many practical rights and obligations are defined by three distinct regional regimes. Pre?existing energy cooperatives remain important vehicles and often act as de?facto energy communities, but they must now navigate both cooperative law and layered EC?specific rules, which can blur the line between “legacy” cooperatives and formally recognised RECs/CECs in empirical mapping
column19: Energy communities must take a standard legal form under Belgian company/association law; in practice, this includes cooperatives, non?profit associations and companies, with municipalities and other public bodies able to participate or co?found entities. Pre?existing citizen energy cooperatives remain a key vehicle, especially in Flanders and Wallonia.
column20: Members and shareholders can include natural persons, local authorities, educational institutions, associations, other energy communities and SMEs, provided that participation in ECs is not their main commercial activity. ECs must be primarily non?profit?oriented (main purpose = environmental, economic or social benefits), and Wallonia explicitly restricts any single member or related group from holding 50% or more of voting rights to preserve autonomy; similar “effective control” safeguards appear in Brussels and Flanders via statute requirements
column21: REC control must be exercised by members located near the production facilities or within the local area defined in regional law or in the EC’s statutes (especially explicit in Wallonia and Brussels), whereas CECs focus more on control by eligible non?large actors and have looser geographical proximity conditions
column22: Participation in ECs is open and voluntary, based on objective and non?discriminatory criteria, and citizens retain their full rights as network users. Regional frameworks require democratic governance and effective control by citizens, municipalities and SMEs (via voting?rights and autonomy rules), which ensures that citizen and local?authority categories collectively dominate decision?making even where there is no explicit numeric threshold beyond Wallonia’s 50% rule.
column23: Local authorities can join and co?own projects as members or shareholders and in some cases initiate ECs, provided they respect autonomy and non?profit?purpose requirements and do not exercise dominant control. Regions also support ECs through regulatory oversight and support schemes, with regulators such as Brugel maintaining EC registers and guidance
column24:
Commercial suppliers, aggregators and service companies may cooperate with ECs, including via project development, operation, billing, data management and flexibility services, and may hold minority stakes as long as they do not undermine autonomy and effective control by citizen and local actors. 
Flemish rules explicitly allow delegation of installation, operation, data processing and maintenance to third parties without those third parties becoming ECs, which facilitates more advanced flexibility? or cVPP?type setups while keeping governance in community hands
column26: Citizen?majority and citizen?municipality?majority co?operatives dominate the Belgian EC landscape, building on a long cooperative tradition, while regional rules tailor autonomy and control tests differently (hard 50% cap in Wallonia, detailed statute?based “effective control” tests in Brussels and Flanders). This combination produces a family resemblance to Austria/Netherlands?style flexibility?oriented regimes in Flanders and to France?style statute?heavy, regulator?supervised regimes in Brussels, with Wallonia somewhere in between.
column27: Yes – energy sharing from renewable sources is permitted in all three regions via legal frameworks for collective self?consumption and energy sharing, implemented through energy communities and, in some cases, peer?to?peer or “two?meter” sharing models that allocate production among participants using the public distribution grid.
column28: Dominant models are collective self?consumption and local energy sharing of PV (and other RES) behind the public distribution grid, with ECs organising allocation while residual supply and imbalance remain with commercial suppliers or delegated balancing?responsible parties.
column29: Energy sharing must occur within a single regional DSO area and is typically constrained by proximity criteria embedded in REC definitions and sharing rules (e.g. local area or feeder level), with Brussels also offering peer?to?peer sharing between two meters within the region; business?to?business sharing remains more constrained than residential and EC?based sharing.
column30: Participants generally keep individual supply contracts, and in several Flemish and Walloon configurations energy sharing currently requires all participants to share the same supplier, who handles residual supply, settlement and market interface, while the EC or organiser manages allocation rules; Brussels allows ECs to share electricity without a supplier licence but they must be balancing?responsible or delegate that role
column31: Energy sharing is subject to strict metering (smart meters with quarter?hourly data), authorisation or registration with regional regulators, and detailed DSO validation of sharing perimeters and allocation rules, with authorisations time?limited (e.g. 5–10 years) and renewable. Key bottlenecks identified in pilots include the need for a common supplier in many cases, region?specific tariffs that can erode economic benefits, and complex choices of sharing and billing rules, all of which increase transaction costs for small ECs
column33: Most Belgian ECs and sharing initiatives rely on default or simple allocation rules (often proportional to consumption or predefined shares) validated by DSOs and regulators, with more advanced dynamic sharing and flexibility use still limited to pilot projects. Regional differences matter: Flanders experiments more with multiple sharing variants (intra?building CSC, peer?to?peer, “self?sharing”), Brussels emphasises regulated EC?based and two?meter sharing under Brugel supervision, and Wallonia uses an explicit authorisation regime where CWaPE approves energy?sharing activities within defined perimeters
column34: Medium to high - digital meters are being rolled out nationwide but on different timelines: Flanders is in the final phase with a target of 100% digital meters by mid?2029, Wallonia aims for full rollout by end?2029, and Brussels plans to equip almost all residents by 2030, with early roll?out and specific groups already covered. Participation in energy?sharing schemes requires a digital/smart meter capable of quarter?hourly measurement
column35: 15?minute data aligned with the balancing period are used for energy?sharing and CSC allocation and are transmitted daily (quarter?hourly series plus monthly totals) from DSOs to suppliers and relevant actors
column36: DSOs collect quarter?hourly consumption and injection data and automatically send them to suppliers for billing and settlement; for energy sharing, DSOs or data hubs also compute or provide allocation data to the organiser/EC and apply the appropriate metering regime. Individual members can access their own data via DSO/supplier portals, and in Brussels specific third?party data?access procedures allow authorised entities (with a mandate) to receive consumption data via secure channels, enabling external service providers to support ECs and building managers
column38: Key barriers include the incomplete rollout of smart meters (especially outside Flanders), the requirement for digital meters as a precondition for joining energy?sharing schemes, and the complexity of data?access and consent procedures for third?party optimisation or cVPP?type services. Academic and policy analyses also highlight that, although 15?minute data are technically available, standardised processes for substitute values, historical data access and cross?regional interoperability remain under development, which can slow down advanced flexibility use cases
column39: Yes – ECs can provide flexibility and aggregation services for both generation and demand?side resources; regional and federal frameworks explicitly list aggregation and participation in flexibility services among EC activities
column40: Independent aggregators (often termed flexibility service providers) are recognised as distinct market participants and can offer services without needing supplier consent, using Belgium’s transfer?of?energy (ToE) mechanism to settle imbalances and energy volumes with suppliers/BRPs. ECs can therefore either rely on independent aggregators for flexibility and market access or work through their existing supplier arrangements
column41: REC and CEC frameworks in all three regions allow ECs themselves to act as aggregators and flexibility providers: they may aggregate members’ generation, storage and flexible demand, participate in flexibility services and offer aggregation to DSOs/TSO or markets, without a separate “community aggregator” licence beyond general market?participant requirements. In practice, many ECs delegate technical and market functions to specialised aggregators or suppliers while retaining strategic control and benefit?sharing rules at community level.
column43: Interaction with DSOs and Elia is still evolving: pilot projects show ECs providing local flexibility (e.g. congestion management, virtual islanding, reserve services), but standard products and procedures for EC?based flexibility are not yet fully mainstreamed. Academic work points to promising roles for “community aggregators” in hosting?capacity enhancement and DSO?contracted services, but highlights transaction?cost and coordination challenges, especially around data, baseline definitions and remuneration models for independent aggregation
column44: ECs are formally recognised as market actors with the right to access electricity markets in a non?discriminatory manner, either directly or via aggregation; they can sell electricity through suppliers/PPAs, access green certificate and other RES support schemes, and, in principle, participate in balancing and emerging local flexibility services. In practice, most ECs operate mainly in retail/self?consumption and support?scheme channels, with flexibility and balancing participation still at pilot or early?stage level
column45: Direct participation of ECs in wholesale day?ahead and intraday markets is legally possible but uncommon; most ECs rely on PPAs with suppliers, sell surplus under support schemes (e.g. green certificates) or work through suppliers/aggregators who hold the necessary market access and balancing responsibilities
column46: Key actors for EC market access include the federal regulator and regional regulators (notably Brugel in Brussels and CWaPE in Wallonia), the TSO Elia, regional DSOs, and community and cooperative federations such as REScoop?linked organisations that provide legal and technical support. Support schemes and policy programmes—such as regional green certificate systems and energy?sharing pilot frameworks—also shape the practical routes to market for ECs.
column48: Belgian transposition emphasises non?discriminatory market access and level?playing?field principles for RECs and CECs, ensuring they are treated like other market participants while retaining consumer rights. However, the absence of fully developed local flexibility markets and the reliance on intermediaries for wholesale and balancing access mean that, at present, ECs’ market participation is structurally biased toward energy?sharing, retail?level optimisation and support schemes rather than direct multi?market engagement
column49: Shared and self?consumed electricity in Belgian ECs still pays network charges; there is no general exemption, but tariffs are meant to be cost?reflective and non?discriminatory, and in Brussels the DSO applies lower network charges for energy shared over shorter grid distances (e.g. within the same substation).
column50: Belgium is moving towards capacity?based distribution tariffs: in Flanders and increasingly elsewhere, part of the grid fee is based on peak demand (“capacity tariff”) and part on kWh consumed, which also applies to EC members. In Brussels, network charges for shared energy are differentiated by grid level and proximity (same building, same MV/LV substation, above substation), with closer sharing attracting lower network?use prices, explicitly to encourage local energy sharing
column51: Energy communities can access general RES support such as regional green certificate schemes and investment grants; in Brussels, all ECs are eligible for the Green Certificates Scheme for exported production, and there are dedicated loan programmes for cooperatives, non?profits and condominium PV. Flanders offers a “green energy call” investment support programme for medium?sized PV and small/medium wind that includes measures for ECs, and at federal level offshore RES tenders are designed to allow EC investment and ownership as part of the tendering process
column53: Recent tariff reforms (capacity?based distribution charges and complex network?charge structures for shared energy) mean that ECs must actively manage peaks and design sharing rules to remain economically viable; empirical work on Belgian pilots finds that network?tariff adjustments or rebates are often needed for energy?sharing communities to break even under “normal” price conditions. At the same time, proximity?based tariff reductions in Brussels and targeted investment support in Flanders create important levers for EC viability, so pricing and support can either significantly enable or undermine EC and cVPP business cases depending on the region and design details
column59: Ambiguous and regionally fragmented rules (e.g. differing proximity definitions, voting?rights safeguards and authorisation procedures) create complexity and uncertainty for EC founders. Some key notions (such as “local perimeter” and detailed conditions for collective self?consumption in Wallonia) remain to be fully specified or harmonised, and supplier?licence requirements still limit straightforward member?to?member sales in many configurations.
column60: Routes to monetise flexibility and local services remain underdeveloped: there is no mature local flexibility market, and EC participation in balancing and ancillary services is largely confined to pilots. Complex tariff structures, PPA arrangements and the need for supplier or aggregator intermediation make it difficult for small ECs to capture the full value of their flexibility and shared generation
column61: Incomplete smart?meter rollout, especially outside Flanders, and the requirement for quarter?hourly digital metering for energy sharing limit who can join ECs and when. Metering and data?management for multi?site or multi?EC participants are complex, with evolving rules around allocation, substitute values and interoperability between regional systems.
column62: Under typical retail price conditions, energy?sharing communities often struggle to break even without specific tariff adjustments or subsidies, as network charges and administrative costs can offset savings from self?consumption. Small citizen projects face high transaction costs relative to project size and can find it difficult to secure bank finance or compete with professional developers for access to the best sites and support schemes.
column63: Awareness and understanding of ECs remain uneven, particularly among low?income households, SMEs and non?energy civil?society actors, limiting the pool of initiators and members. Many initiatives rely on volunteers and a small core group of motivated individuals, leading to capacity constraints and burnout risks, while concerns about “corporate capture” can create mistrust when commercial actors are involved.
column64: Spatial and ownership constraints (e.g. fragmented building ownership, landlord?tenant issues, limited rooftop suitability) hinder the formation of ECs in dense urban areas and mixed?use neighbourhoods. Grid constraints and connection delays in some areas also slow down new RES and storage projects that could underpin ECs or cVPPs
column65: There is strong policy interest in ECs and energy sharing across all three regions, with emerging calls for projects, advisory services, tariff pilots and investment support tailored to community initiatives, plus a dense network of cooperative and NGO actors providing expertise. Academic and policy analyses stress that targeted reforms—simplifying procedures, refining tariffs for local sharing and flexibility, and strengthening non?profit/anti?capture safeguards—could unlock significant additional EC and cVPP potential in Belgium’s already dynamic community?energy ecosystem.

column2: Wind?dominated, decentralised electricity system with strong district heating and combined heat-and-power integration, high interconnection to Nordic and European neighbours, and a long-term goal of fully renewable, fossil?free energy by 2050.
column3: Fully liberalised “supplier?centric” electricity market: since 2013 end?users contract only with competitive suppliers, who interface with Energinet as TSO and geographically bounded DSOs; entry barriers for new retailers are relatively low but incumbents and large cooperatives remain influential
column4: Very high renewable penetration led by wind: wind power represents roughly half of Danish electricity supply and Denmark has one of the highest per?capita wind outputs globally; bioenergy, waste and increasingly large?scale solar thermal dominate district?heating renewables, with solar PV expanding from a lower base.
column5: State?owned TSO Energinet operates the transmission grid and interconnectors; electricity distribution is handled by multiple local DSOs with geographic monopolies, many municipally or cooperatively owned, while almost all district?heating networks are run by cooperatives or municipalities, reinforcing local control over infrastructure.
column6: At least several hundred community?energy initiatives, including 527 identified energy cooperatives and community projects, with some wind and at least 325 district?heating cooperatives (i.e TEC - Thermal Energy Communities) ; no single, consolidated national EC registry exists yet
column7: No explicitly labelled community virtual power plants identified; community projects focus on ownership of generation (especially wind and heating), with flexibility and aggregation mostly handled by suppliers, balance responsible parties and larger commercial aggregators
column8: Predominantly onshore and near?shore wind, biomass and waste?fired combined heat-and-power, district?heating systems increasingly integrating large?scale solar thermal and heat pumps, and growing but still smaller?scale solar PV

column11: Yes – Renewable Energy Communities are defined in the Law on the Promotion of Renewable Energy and in a 2021 Executive Order, which sets out a REC definition aligned with RED II (open and voluntary participation, autonomy, effective control by local members) and anchors it in primary law but operationalises key details via secondary legislation.
column12: Yes – Citizen Energy Communities are defined together with RECs in the same Executive Order under the Electricity Supply Act; the CEC definition mirrors the EU electricity?market directive criteria (open and voluntary, effective control by non?large actors) but does not include a geographical proximity requirement and is thus framed as a distinct electricity?market category alongside RECs
column13: Partial – Denmark has introduced REC and CEC definitions in primary and secondary legislation and allowed electricity sharing, but several RED II/ED elements remain weak or missing: the supportive enabling framework is underdeveloped, exemptions from balance responsibility and supplier obligations are limited, and implementation of EC?specific rights in support schemes and tariffs is still incomplete
column14: RECs and CECs may produce, consume, store and share electricity via the public grid and participate in the electricity market as consumers, producers, electricity trading companies or aggregators, but for all activities other than the shared electricity itself they must comply with the full set of obligations applicable to regular suppliers and traders; they have no explicit right to own or operate public distribution networks and must generally contract with a licensed supplier to handle billing, balancing and market interface unless they themselves become a fully licensed trading company
column15: Yes – REC and CEC provisions have been introduced through revisions of the Law on the Promotion of Renewable Energy and the Electricity Supply Act, supplemented by an Executive Order that jointly defines RECs and CECs and additional orders on electricity sharing and support grants for local community projects, but there is no single consolidated “energy communities act
column16: No separate EC registry exists; RECs and CECs must be set up in standard legal forms (association, partnership, cooperative or company), demonstrate compliance with REC/CEC criteria, notify DSOs and contract with an electricity trading company for sharing, and they face essentially the same licensing, balancing and supplier?obligation requirements as conventional market actors if they want to supply or trade electricity themselves, which creates significant administrative burdens for small citizen groups.

column18: Denmark has layered REC/CEC definitions onto a long?standing cooperative and municipal ownership landscape without creating a strongly differentiated rights regime for energy communities: while RECs and CECs are legally recognised and can engage in electricity sharing, many of their rights and obligations are treated as equivalent to those of regular suppliers and aggregators, and key supportive elements (simplified licensing, balance?responsibility exemptions, EC?specific tariff rules) remain underdeveloped or delegated to future secondary legislation.
column19: Associations, partnerships, cooperatives (andelsselskaber / co-ops), and capital companies (e.g. limited companies); energy communities typically use cooperative or association forms, but can also be organised as limited?liability companies.
column20: Members and owners of RECs/CECs can be natural persons, SMEs, local authorities and other legal entities; effective control must not be exercised by large enterprises or energy companies, and REC/CEC rules require that decisive influence remains with local citizens, small actors and public bodies, with voting and ownership structures designed to prevent capture by large commercial players
column21: For Renewable Energy Communities, effective control is expected to be exercised by members located in proximity to the RES projects (same or nearby area without specific distance). Citizen Energy Communities do not have a strict geographical proximity requirement and may include members from across Denmark as long as control remains with eligible small actors.
column22: Energy communities are open to citizen membership through cooperative shares or association membership, with one?member?one?vote or similar democratic rules common in co?ops and associations; historically, Danish wind and district?heating cooperatives have mobilised large numbers of local citizens as co?owners
column23: Municipalities and other local public bodies can join RECs and CECs as members or co?owners and continue Denmark’s long tradition of municipal involvement in energy: many DSOs and district?heating companies are municipally or cooperatively owned, and several recent community projects have been initiated, co?developed or strategically supported by municipalities seeking local climate and energy goals
column24: Commercial RES developers, large utilities and professional service providers frequently co?develop or operate wind, solar and heating projects alongside citizen and municipal investors; under REC/CEC rules they may participate as members or service providers but are restricted from exercising decisive control, and licensed suppliers/trading companies typically handle market interface, billing, balancing and data management for energy?sharing or flexibility services offered by communities

column26: Market conditions and concentration in the wind sector mean that many newer projects involve significant commercial partners, and activists have criticised a shift from genuinely citizen?led to more corporate?dominated ownership structures
column27: Yes - regulations on energy sharing permit electricity sharing within a single building such as a housing cooperative, but electricity sharing outside of a building is only possible through the collective grid and is subject to the general tariffs and taxes.
column28:
Energy communities exist as eco-villages, small-scale domestic heating systems in rural communities, and cooperatives focusing on local wind and solar panels on residential buildings.
Electricity sharing is implemented as collective self-consumption / virtual allocation of local renewable production, with the energy community or its representative defining sharing coefficients while a licensed electricity trading company supplies residual demand and handles market settlement.
column29: Behind-the-meter models are confined to one building or common connection point, while grid-based electricity sharing is currently limited to local use within the same distribution grid area and is still being operationalised, with no widely used large-radius model comparable to the 20 km schemes seen in some other EU countries.
column30: Participants in Danish RECs/CECs must have, or be covered by, a contract with a licensed electricity trading company: electricity sharing takes place under this supply contract, which covers both shared volumes and any additional consumption, and if the community itself wishes to act as supplier it's possible but  it must obtain a full trading licence and comply with all supplier obligations
column31: Electricity sharing is legally enabled but constrained by high regulatory and contractual complexity: RECs/CECs must arrange supplier intermediation even though suppliers are not obliged to serve them, all standard grid tariffs and taxes still apply to shared electricity, and there are no dedicated, lower “local sharing” tariffs; DSOs are formally required to cooperate where sharing can reduce grid load, but in practice administrative barriers and lack of clear procedures mean that many initiatives report difficulties in obtaining cooperation and some projects have been abandoned

column33: energy sharing is allowed only via supplier-mediated models on the existing grid, with full application of tariffs and taxes and no strong EC-specific incentives, so most existing community activity still centres on traditional generation and district heating rather than on large-scale, grid-based energy sharing and energy services
column34: ?80 to 100% rollout (2020); smart meters are now standard for virtually all Danish electricity customers, with DSOs having replaced legacy meters and integrated them into the national DataHub
column35: 15?minute data resolution for settlement and market processes, in line with the 15?minute balancing and settlement period introduced in the Danish market; DataHub processes detailed interval data for all metering points
column36: DSOs collect meter data and send it to the central DataHub operated by Energinet; suppliers and other authorised market participants access the interval data they need for billing and settlement via DataHub, while end?users can view their own consumption and price information through supplier portals or the national eloverblik.dk interface, and energy communities or their representatives can receive aggregated and allocation data when acting as authorised market parties
column38: Denmark’s combination of near?universal smart metering and a mature, centralised DataHub significantly reduces technical data barriers for energy communities and flexibility services compared to other countries. Remaining challenges relate more to regulatory design (e.g. tariff structures, supplier obligations, roles of independent aggregators) than to basic metering or data availability
column39: Yes – aggregation of both generation and demand?side flexibility is allowed under general electricity?market rules, and RECs/CECs may in principle act as aggregators or contract with aggregators for participation in wholesale and ancillary?services markets
column40: Independent aggregators separate from suppliers are recognised in Danish market design, especially through the Market Model 3.0 reforms, which relax earlier requirements to link aggregators to a specific retailer/BRP; however, in practice independent aggregation is still emerging and subject to contractual arrangements with balance responsible parties, with relatively few fully independent aggregators active so far
column41: Energy communities can, in principle, provide aggregation services themselves by becoming licensed market actors (aggregators or trading companies) or by partnering with existing aggregators; there is no separate “community aggregator” licence or simplified regime, so ECs face the same technical, forecasting and balancing requirements as other aggregators, and most current Danish ECs focus on ownership and local sharing rather than on direct participation in ancillary?services markets as aggregators

column44: Energy communities can participate in the Danish market mainly by owning generation and selling output via standard channels (feed?in contracts, PPAs or direct marketing through suppliers/traders), by acting as customers on retail tariffs (including dynamic tariffs) and, where they or their partners qualify, by providing demand?side flexibility or generation to balancing and ancillary?services markets; there is no dedicated local flexibility market specifically for ECs, and ECs access existing national markets under general rules.
column45: Direct wholesale market participation is legally possible for ECs that become licensed trading companies, but in practice most Danish energy communities sell power indirectly via PPAs or standard supplier arrangements and do not themselves register as balance responsible parties or direct wholesale participants
column46: Key actors for EC market access are the Danish Utility Regulator (Forsyningstilsynet) as energy regulator, Energinet as TSO and DataHub operator, local DSOs as grid operators, competitive suppliers and aggregators as market intermediaries (40+), and national/community organisations and programmes that support citizen ownership and REC/CEC implementation. The main public bodies regulating and supervising the Danish energy market are the Danish energy agency (DEA), responsible for tasks linked to energy production, supply, and consumption, and the Danish Utility Regulator (DUR), responsible for securing consumer interests in the utility sectors. Both agencies answer to the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Utilities.
column48: Market rules formally guarantee non?discriminatory access to wholesale and balancing markets and to DataHub for all eligible market participants, including energy communities acting through suppliers or as licensed traders; however, Denmark has not created specific priority?access, reduced?tariff or simplified?licensing provisions for ECs, so their market access conditions are essentially the same as for other small generators and consumers, with suppliers and aggregators acting as gatekeepers in practice.
column49: Shared and self-consumed electricity in ECs is generally treated like other consumption and pays standard distribution network tariffs on imports from the grid (volumetric grid charges plus fixed components), but a 2023 amendment to the Electricity Supply Act allows DSOs to introduce reduced and geographically localised grid tariffs for local associations of users, including energy communities, where their use of the grid demonstrably reduces network costs; these EC-specific reductions depend on DSO tariff methodologies approved by the Danish Supply Authority and are not yet widely implemented in practice
column50: DSO tariffs typically combine a fixed subscription/connection component with volumetric øre/kWh charges (and increasingly time-of-use or dynamic elements), differentiated by voltage level and customer segment; for small prosumers and EC members, distribution charges are calculated on gross electricity drawn from the grid plus a small availability fee, so even when they have rooftop PV or participate in an EC they still contribute to grid costs in broadly the same way as comparable non-generating customers
column51: Renewable generation owned by ECs primarily relies on technology-specific premiums and competitive tenders under the Promotion of Renewable Energy Act (VE-Lov), with feed-in premiums or contracts-for-difference paid on top of market prices up to capped budgets; in parallel, Order BEK 1162/2022, updated by BEK 451/2024, establishes EC-specific grants for local energy communities and local anchoring of the climate transition, funding both information projects (DKK 10 000–200 000) and larger demonstration projects (DKK 20 000–750 000) that involve generation, sharing, storage, flexibility, aggregation or renewable heating/cooling and aim to strengthen long-term local engagement.
column53: In Denmark, generic RES support (premiums and tenders) is technology- and project-based rather than EC-specific, while network tariffs remain largely cost-reflective and applied to ECs on the same basis as other customers; the new legal option for reduced, localised tariffs and targeted EC grants improves the enabling framework on paper, but the lack of broadly implemented EC-local tariffs and the move away from fixed feed-in schemes towards competitive tenders and dynamic tariffs mean that small citizen projects still face tight margins and depend heavily on good PPAs, strong local organisation and access to grant funding to remain financially viable
column59:
Except for the electricity that is shared, REC and CEC must comply with all obligations the existing grid suppliers have, restricting the size and efficiency of renewable energy installations that can be established by RECs and CECs. The Ministry may also lay down rules exempting CEC from certain rules and obligations associated with electricity supply obligations and aggregation to its participants and capital owners, but they have not yet done so.
Production and supply – not just distribution – are required to be unbundled from each other. This could prevent energy communities, at least in the electricity sector, from being able to fully exercise their rights.
Complex supplier, balance-responsibility and market-participation rules for ECs; ECs cannot own or operate distribution networks and must rely on licensed trading companies for electricity sharing, which also limits autonomous operation.
column60: In an Executive Order, it is stated that DSOs are obliged to cooperate with RECs and CECs in cases where their activity can reduce the load on the grid. In practice, it has been very difficult to make DSOs comply with this regulation, leading to several cases where RECs and CECs have given up due to administrative barriers. Electricity sharing in REC and CEC takes place under an agreement on the supply of electricity with an electricity trading company, which handles offsetting and distribution based on their needs. This supply contract includes both the shared energy consumed and the additional electricity needed to cover the demand. Should the EC decides to fulfill itself the requirement for an agreement, it must comply with all the obligations for the performance of electricity trade business.
column61: Electricity sharing requires full integration with DataHub processes and Energy Track and Trace guarantees of origin, creating technical and IT requirements for small citizen groups despite the near?universal smart-meter rollout
column62: Larger, professional actors are favored by the competitive tenders and market-linked premiums. EC specific tariffs reductions are technically feasible yet they have yet to be implemented. DSOs/suppliers control most of the market activity, while EC bear the greater financial burden and risks. No real financial viability/business models for EC, and there is no true financial incentive for energy sharing or flexibility services
column63: Legacy of strong citizen and municipal ownership coexists (large wind farms and TECs) with a shift towards more corporate-dominated wind and solar projects. Awareness of ECs, organisational capacity and resources are concentrated in already active communities while less organized or lower-income groups are underrepresented in EC initiatives.
column64: Planning and siting constraints for wind and solar (land-use, landscape and local acceptability issues) can limit opportunities for new citizen-led projects even where legal and financial frameworks exist
column65: Simple registration regime as EC. Flexibility reform with Model 3.0, mandatory accession to DSO if alleviates grid pressure (in theory)  and a recent option for reduced, localised grid tariffs.
