column2: Liberalised, meshed continental system with strong cross?border interconnections and a historically centralised “Big Four” utility structure, now complemented by hundreds of municipal utilities and citizen?led RES actors.
column3: Fully liberalised wholesale and retail market with unbundled TSOs and DSOs, competitive suppliers and balancing?responsible parties, though generation and retail remain relatively concentrated among a few large companies alongside many smaller municipal and citizen players.
column4: High and still growing renewable share under the Energiewende, with wind (onshore and offshore) and solar PV as main sources; RES benefit from EEG?based support (now mainly market premiums and tenders) and priority grid access, and private individuals and farmers still own a substantial share of RES capacity
column5: Multiple TSOs (e.g. 50Hertz, Amprion, TenneT, TransnetBW) operate the transmission network, while a large number of DSOs—including many municipal utilities—run local distribution grids; DSOs handle most RES feed?in, and municipal ownership remains significant despite past consolidation and privatisation waves.
column6: Around 1?750 community?energy initiatives identified (including energy cooperatives and other citizen?led organisations), with roughly 896 energy cooperatives active by 2020; Germany has the largest number of such initiatives among JRC case?study countries.
column7: No national category of cVPPs; most community initiatives focus on generation, supply and, in some cases, local optimisation or pilot?scale flexibility services rather than fully fledged community virtual power plants.
column8: Energy cooperatives are mainly active in solar PV (around 80% of projects), with significant participation in onshore wind and some activity in heat, bioenergy and local supply; many projects feed into public grids under EEG support rather than operating as pure self?consumption schemes.
column11: Yes - Germany has aligned its long?standing “Citizen Energy Company” (Bürgerenergiegesellschaft) concept in the Renewable Energies Law (EEG 2023) with the Renewable Energy Community definition in RED II; the Citizen Energy Company definition now applies to onshore wind and PV and governs access to market premiums, exemptions from auction participation and a dedicated grant?to?loan investment. Feb 2026: comprehensive amendment to Energy Industry Act (EnWG) which formally allows energy-sharing (although includes strong supplier/aggregator obligations).
column12: No - Germany has not transposed the Citizen Energy Community definition (IEMD) as a separate legal category; there is currently no stand?alone CEC status in national electricity law, although EnWG reforms (including new energy?sharing provisions in Feb 2026) introduce elements that are relevant for CEC?type activities without using the label
column13: Partial – Germany has a REC?equivalent definition in EEG 2023 via the Citizen Energy Company (Bürgerenergiegesellschaft) and has begun to introduce an energy?sharing regime in EnWG, but it lacks a clear CEC definition and a fully integrated enabling framework that comprehensively sets out EC rights, obligations and barrier?removal duties across the electricity system
column14: Citizen Energy Companies under EEG 2023 have specific rights linked to RES support schemes: eligible onshore wind projects up to 18 MW and PV projects up to 6 MW can receive fixed feed?in tariffs or market premiums without participating in competitive tenders if they notify the Federal Network Agency within strict deadlines, and qualifying projects can access a federal grant?to?loan investment fund for early?stage wind development; beyond these scheme?based rights, ECs operate under general market, grid?access and data rules in EEG and EnWG.
column15: The CEC can be considering a dedicated framework although there is no single “Energy Communities Act”; rather, the framework is spread across the Renewable Energies Law (EEG 2023 via the Citizen Energy Company definition), the Energy Industry Act (EnWG) for market rules and emerging energy?sharing provisions, and the Cooperatives Act (GenG) for the many energy cooperatives that pre?date the Clean Energy Package and still operate as such.
column16: Citizen Energy Companies must comply with both the general requirements of their legal form (e.g. cooperative registration and auditing duties under GenG) and with EEG?specific conditions for Citizen Energy Company status (minimum 50 natural?person members, 75% local voting rights within 50 km, SME/municipal limits for non?natural members, 10% cap per member), and they must notify the Federal Network Agency within three weeks of key permitting or commissioning milestones to secure tender exemptions, feed?in tariffs and access to the wind investment fund; other community initiatives that do not seek Citizen Energy Company privileges operate under general cooperative and company law but do not benefit from these scheme?linked advantages.
column18: Germany’s EC legal framework is layered on long?standing cooperative and municipal practice: hundreds of energy cooperatives continue to operate under the Cooperatives Act, while EEG 2023 formally aligns the Citizen Energy Company with RED II’s REC concept to structure access to premiums, tender exemptions and wind?project investment support; at the same time, Germany has deliberately not introduced a separate CEC definition and still lacks a unified EC statute, so many rights and obligations remain embedded in general EEG/EnWG provisions rather than in a dedicated energy?community title
column19: German energy communities use several company forms: GbR (Gesellschaft bürgerlichen Rechts) with very low administrative burdens and no minimum capital but unlimited liability of members; GmbH & Co. KG, typically chosen for larger investments with liability limited to each partner’s capital share; and, most importantly, the registered cooperative (eingetragene Genossenschaft, eG), which is now the most common legal form for energy communities, subject to the Cooperatives Act and pre?registration scrutiny of the business plan and statutes by a cooperative association, making it relatively insolvency?proof though more capital? and admin?intensive than a GbR.
column20: Citizen Energy Companies must consist of at least 50 natural persons with voting rights; at least 75% of voting rights must be held by natural persons living within 50 km of the installation, non?natural voting rights are restricted to SMEs and municipal local authorities, and no member or shareholder may hold more than 10% of voting rights, ensuring dispersed, citizen?dominated ownership and preventing capture by single large investors.
column21: For Citizen Energy Companies, at least 75% of voting rights must be held by natural persons registered with a dwelling in postcode areas wholly or partly within a 50 km radius of the planned RES installation, so effective control is tied to local residents; there is no additional grid?topology perimeter (e.g. LV/MV) for governance, and other community energy initiatives (e.g. co?ops outside the EEG definition) are not legally bound by this 50 km rule.
column22: Citizen Energy Companies and energy cooperatives are explicitly designed around broad citizen participation: the EEG definition requires a minimum number of local natural?person members with effective influence in shareholder meetings, while cooperative law typically implements one?member?one?vote and democratic governance; historically, German energy co?ops have mobilised thousands of local citizens and farmers as members and small?scale investors in PV, wind and bioenergy projects.
column23: Municipalities and their associations can participate as minority shareholders in Citizen Energy Companies under EEG 2023, but effective control must lie with local natural persons: at least 75% of voting rights must be held by natural persons residing within 50 km of the plant, and no member (including a municipality) may hold more than 10% of voting rights, so public actors cannot control a Citizen Energy Company; beyond this scheme-specific role, municipalities and Stadtwerke are important partners and co-owners in many energy cooperatives and joint projects, yet Germany has not created a separate CEC category, so there is no CEC-specific public-actor role in national law
column24: Commercial developers, project companies and professional service providers frequently partner with Citizen Energy Companies and energy cooperatives for project development, grid connection and tender participation, but the EEG’s membership, locality and 10% ownership?cap rules limit their formal control; third parties can still play significant technical and financial roles, yet effective governance must remain with dispersed local citizen and municipal members for projects to qualify as Citizen Energy Companies
column26: German community?energy governance builds on these legal forms and long?standing cooperative traditions: most mature ECs are organised as eG cooperatives with one?member?one?vote and pre?checked statutes, while smaller or early?stage initiatives may start as low?cost GbR partnerships and larger, more capital?intensive projects sometimes use GmbH & Co. KG structures; the EEG’s Citizen Energy Company definition then superimposes additional criteria (minimum 50 local natural?person members, 75% local voting rights, 10% cap per member) for those entities that want to qualify for community?specific support schemes, but many energy?community?like cooperatives continue to operate under general GenG/EEG rules without adopting the formal Citizen Energy Company status.
column27: Yes, but in two different ways: (i) building-level “tenant electricity” (Mieterstrom) and communal building supply, where PV power is supplied to consumers in the same or adjacent building without using the public grid under §?21(3) EEG and §§?42a–b EnWG; and, from 1 June 2026 onward, (ii) grid-based “energy sharing” under the new §?42c EnWG, which allows groups of final customers to jointly use renewable electricity via the public distribution network within the same grid area, with virtual allocation based on smart-meter data.
column28: German community energy now operates four main model types: (1) classical EEG-supported RES plants (often owned by co?ops or Citizen Energy Companies) feeding all output into the grid; (2) regional green-supply models where co?ops or Stadtwerke act as suppliers to local customers; (3) behind-the-meter tenant electricity and communal building-supply schemes, where the plant operator supplies tenants in the same/adjacent building without using the public grid; and (4) emerging §?42c EnWG “energy sharing” schemes, where a designated organiser coordinates the joint use of local renewable production by multiple customers via the public distribution grid, with virtual allocation and quarter-hourly metering.
column29: Tenant electricity and communal building-supply schemes are constrained to one building or several residential buildings in the same neighbourhood without using the public grid, with plant capacities typically up to 100 kW and minimum residential shares; by contrast, §?42c EnWG energy sharing is building-overlapping and tied to the same distribution-grid area (Netzgebiet) of a DSO, so participants and the RES plant must lie within the same DSO network, but there is no explicit kilometre-radius limit—geographical scope is effectively defined by the DSO’s concession area and metering/information-technology capabilities
column30:
Overall, the sale of electricity to retail customers is associated with a number of legal obligations and tasks that require professional corporate structures.
In tenant-electricity and communal building-supply models, the installation operator already acts as an electricity supplier to tenants, handling billing and contracts while the public grid is bypassed; in §?42c EnWG energy sharing, an “energy sharing organiser” (which may be a co?op, Citizen Energy Company or other entity) assumes supplier-like responsibilities—concluding contracts with participating customers and the plant operator, managing billing, handling market communication and data exchange with DSOs and metering-point operators, and coordinating with residual suppliers that continue to serve non-shared consumption
column31: While §?42c EnWG is a legal milestone, regulatory and technical complexity remains a major bottleneck: energy sharing depends on smart-meter rollout and quarter-hourly data exchange, requires communities to comply with supplier-like licensing, consumer-protection and market-process rules, and currently offers only limited tariff advantages (no broad exemption from network charges or levies), so many small citizen groups may find classic EEG feed-in or tenant electricity models simpler and economically more attractive in the short term.
column33:
Germany has moved from a framework where community energy relied on joint RES ownership, regional retail and tightly constrained tenant-electricity schemes with no grid-based sharing, to one where §?42c EnWG finally provides a formal basis for “Energy Sharing Communities” using the public distribution grid from mid-2026 onwards; however, unlike frontrunners such as Austria; the German model is currently characterised by high organisational and IT requirements, modest financial incentives and a strong focus on active customers rather than a dedicated REC/CEC category, so its transformative potential for energy communities will depend on future adjustments to tariffs, support schemes and administrative procedures.

Pilot projects and conceptual work (e.g. Ehrtmann et al.) show that German ECs can use digital platforms and blockchain-based governance to implement P2P sharing within the constraints of current law, but these models remain niche and depend on existing supplier or self-consumption arrangements rather than a dedicated legal P2P framework

National smart?meter rollout is legally mandated but still in an early phase: only around 3–4% of metering points were equipped with intelligent metering systems by 2025–26, yet amendments to the Metering Point Operation Act (MsbG) now require default metering operators to equip at least 20% of eligible high?consumption and controllable?load customers with smart meters by end?2025 and 90% of these mandatory points by 2032, with the Bundesnetzagentur already opening supervisory proceedings against operators that failed to reach the 20% quota.
column35: Where smart meters and smart?meter gateways are installed, they provide at least 15?minute consumption and generation data as the standard settlement interval, with legal requirements for near?real?time access and 15?minute data availability for customers and authorised third parties, which is essential for dynamic tariffs, §?42c EnWG energy sharing and flexibility services.
column36: Smart?meter gateway rules and data?protection law give final customers the right to access their own consumption and generation data and to authorise third parties (suppliers, aggregators, energy?management services or energy?sharing organisers) to receive these data under strict security and privacy standards; in practice, complex SMGW procedures and heterogeneous IT capabilities among DSOs and metering?point operators still limit how easily energy communities and Citizen Energy Companies can access and use granular data for local optimisation and energy sharing.
column38: Germany has a technically sophisticated but slow and administratively complex smart?meter and data?access regime: advanced SMGWs can provide the 15?minute data needed for energy sharing and flexibility, yet low penetration rates, heterogeneous rollout among DSOs and strict security requirements mean that many energy communities still rely on a mix of conventional meters, partial smart?meter coverage and data solutions rather than a seamless nationwide digital infrastructure.
column39:
Yes – aggregation of generation, load and flexibility is allowed and fully integrated into the German market design: aggregators can participate in wholesale markets and balancing services under general EnWG and market?rule provisions, and neither Citizen Energy Companies nor other community actors are legally prevented from acting as aggregators, although there is no dedicated “community aggregator” status.
Aggregation is also happening when energy communities favor the regional balancing pool business model. The regional renewable energy capacities are aggregated and balanced via a separate regional balancing pool provided by the energy supplier which gives the technical infrastructure, sets up the balancing pool, and defines its geographical expansions.
column40: Independent aggregation—where an aggregator pools resources without being the supplier of record—is permitted in principle under the German implementation of EU market rules, but practical uptake remains limited and subject to complex coordination, imbalance?settlement and data?exchange arrangements between aggregators, suppliers and DSOs; there is no special, simplified regime for energy communities that want to act as independent aggregators
column41: In practice, some German energy cooperatives and Citizen Energy Companies are beginning to explore aggregation-like roles—such as optimising local PV, storage and controllable loads, participating in flexibility pilots, or acting as intermediaries for dynamic tariffs—but most community actors still focus on generation and supply rather than operating as full?fledged aggregators in wholesale or balancing markets, partly because of the technical, regulatory and IT complexity involved

column43: Aggregation in Germany is legally open to energy communities on equal terms with other market participants, but the combination of slow smart?meter rollout, complex market rules for independent aggregators and the absence of EC?specific facilitation means that, so far, aggregation remains primarily a domain of specialised commercial providers and larger utilities rather than a core activity of most Citizen Energy Companies or cooperatives, which continue to prioritise project development and local supply
column44: Energy communities and Citizen Energy Companies access markets mainly via standard pathways: EEG support schemes (feed?in tariffs and market premiums with tender exemptions for qualifying Bürgerenergiegesellschaften), bilateral PPAs and participation in wholesale and balancing markets through suppliers, direct marketers or aggregators; the new §?42c EnWG regime adds local energy?sharing as an additional, albeit administratively demanding, avenue for valorising local RES production.

column48: Germany offers relatively mature market?access routes for community?owned RES via EEG support and PPAs, but communities seeking to move beyond “plain” generation into local flexibility, aggregation or energy sharing still face substantial complexity in grid access, metering, data exchange and market processes and for the great majority have to become a DSO or supplier themselves, or entrust these services to other incumbent/professional actors.
column49: Electricity network charges in Germany are regulated at national level by the Bundesnetzagentur and represent a substantial share of final household prices; they are largely volumetric but include capacity and time-differentiated components, and they apply broadly and non-discriminatorily to all users, with no dedicated reductions or exemptions for energy communities, Citizen Energy Companies or energy-sharing schemes beyond generally applicable rules.
column50: Distribution tariffs are structured according to national guidelines but set and collected by DSOs, combining fixed elements (e.g. basic fees linked to connection capacity and metering) with variable energy charges that may vary by voltage level and, increasingly, by time of use; recent debates and consultation papers on adapting distribution tariffs (“AgNes”) highlight possible future moves towards more locational- and flexibility-oriented pricing, yet energy communities and Citizen Energy Companies currently face the same DSO tariff structures as other customers, and any locational benefits remain at pilot or discussion stage rather than being codified as EC-specific distribution pricing.
column51: Germany’s main financial schemes for community energy are provided through EEG 2023 and related programmes: small RES plants (up to 100 kW) can receive fixed feed-in tariffs, larger projects obtain sliding market premiums on top of market revenues, and Citizen Energy Companies benefit from tender-exempt fixed tariffs for onshore wind projects up to 18 MW and PV projects up to 6 MW that meet strict EEG criteria, as well as from a dedicated federal investment fund that covers up to 70% of eligible pre-development costs (up to EUR 300,000) for citizen wind projects up to 25 MW per applicant under a grant-to-loan model; there is currently no national operating-support or investment scheme targeted specifically at §?42c EnWG energy-sharing communities, which must rely on these generic RES schemes plus standard project finance and municipal or regional programmes.

column53: For energy-sharing communities under §?42c EnWG (too recent to have any scheme associated), Germanwatch stresses that the sharing price must at least match or exceed the EEG support level once all taxes, levies and network charges are deducted, but modelling and expert assessments indicate that, given current tariff structures and high IT and transaction costs (quarter-hourly settlement, billing, data exchange), most Energy Sharing Communities will not be economically viable without additional targeted support or tariff relief—especially for small plants under 100 kW—although simplified supplier duties for sub?30/100 kW projects could reduce costs, and future reforms of network tariffs or dedicated energy-sharing subsidies could substantially change this assessment.
column54: German energy communities offer new avenues for local participation and co-decision, but in practice participation is skewed: surveys and case studies show that governance structures are often dominated by older, well-educated, higher-income men, with high time and knowledge requirements for active roles, and limited involvement of tenants, low-income households and marginalised groups; in the absence of explicit regulatory incentives or support for inclusive outreach, many communities focus on running projects efficiently rather than adapting meeting formats, communication and decision-making to lower participation thresholds, so procedural justice (open access, voice, influence) is only partially realised and depends heavily on the specific initiative and on whether municipalities or intermediaries actively support inclusive governance.

column59: Germany has only partially transposed the EU energy-community acquis: there is no CEC definition, the Citizen Energy Company concept is tightly linked to EEG support rather than to broad rights in networks and markets, and the new §?42c EnWG energy-sharing regime is framed narrowly around small customers with complex supplier duties, quarter-hour balancing and contract requirements; combined with overlapping Mieterstrom rules and general cooperative/company law, this creates a fragmented, hard-to-navigate legal environment for ECs, storage and cVPPs.
column60: Energy communities and Citizen Energy Companies compete in a market dominated by large utilities and professional direct marketers, face high transaction costs to access wholesale, balancing and flexibility markets, and must navigate supplier licensing, direct-marketing obligations and complex retail processes; for energy sharing, Germanwatch and others find that, under current tariffs and market rules, most Energy Sharing Communities will not be profitable without additional support or network-tariff relief, so uptake may remain limited to niches and pilot projects rather than scaling to system-relevant levels.
column61: Slow and uneven smart-meter rollout, coupled with complex smart-meter gateway requirements and heterogeneous DSO IT systems, hampers the data-driven operation of energy communities, storage and cVPPs: only a small share of meters are currently “smart”, quarter-hourly metering and data exchange are not yet ubiquitous, and studies point to Germany’s delayed rollout as a major drag on digital innovation and integration of distributed resources; implementing §?42c energy sharing or sophisticated P2P and flexibility models therefore requires advanced metering and data-exchange infrastructures that many DSOs and communities do not yet have in place
column62: High upfront investment costs, exposure to volatile wholesale prices, the dominance of taxes, levies and network charges in retail tariffs, and the absence of strong energy-community-specific financial incentives or tariff reductions create significant economic barriers: energy communities and tenant-electricity projects often rely on avoiding high retail prices rather than receiving generous support, while Germanwatch and techno-economic studies report that many tenant-electricity and §?42c energy-sharing configurations in multi-family buildings or small ESCs are only marginally profitable—or not viable at all—under current support and tariff structures, especially for low-income groups with limited ability to invest.
column63: German energy communities still tend to be socially selective: survey and case-study evidence shows overrepresentation of older, male, higher-income and higher-education groups in cooperative membership and leadership, substantial time and knowledge requirements for active participation, and limited inclusion of tenants, low-income households and marginalised groups; gender-focused research further highlights that male-dominated organisational cultures, financial-investment framing and technical language deter many women and people prioritising social and environmental over financial motives from engaging in energy communities and emerging P2P models.
column64: Additional barriers include complex and sometimes slow grid-connection procedures, limited municipal capacity and expertise to initiate or support community projects, uncertainty around long-term policy stability (e.g. future EEG reforms, changing subsidy levels), and the risk that commercial actors appropriate the “community” label without genuinely democratic governance; these factors can deter new initiatives, especially in less wealthy regions and smaller municipalities where administrative and financial resources are scarce
column65: At the same time, Germany offers significant opportunities: a large and experienced landscape of energy cooperatives and citizen projects, strong municipal utilities, ambitious renewable targets under EEG 2023/2027 and climate law, and now a formal legal basis for energy sharing under §?42c EnWG; if smart-meter rollout accelerates, if network tariffs and support schemes are adjusted to reward local flexibility and sharing, and if targeted capacity-building and inclusion measures are implemented, energy communities and cVPP-like configurations could leverage Germany’s dense grid, high RES potential and existing cooperative infrastructure to provide local flexibility, reduce grid expansion needs, democratise ownership and enhance energy justice.

column40: Independent aggregators are recognised in French market design, but the EC framework does not create a separate “community aggregator” category; ECs must comply with standard aggregation and balancing rules.
column41: CEC definition explicitly allows provision of aggregation and other energy services; ECs may aggregate members’ load or generation but do so under the same regulatory conditions as any other market actor.
column43: For CECs, French law assigns financial responsibility for imbalances caused by the community: the CEC must either act as a balance responsible party or delegate this responsibility to a third party. This creates a potential risk and capability barrier for EC-run aggregation, since direct market participation requires compliance with RTE’s balance-responsibility framework, financial guarantees, metering/data processes and imbalance-settlement exposure. In practice, community aggregation is therefore likely to depend on delegation to an established BRP, supplier, aggregator or flexibility operator. This creates an important constraint for cVPP development: a community-based VPP could theoretically aggregate local generation, demand response, storage or EV flexibility, but direct operation would require BRP/market-interface capabilities. Delegated aggregation is therefore the more realistic pathway for most French ECs, unless the community develops substantial technical, financial and compliance capacity.
column44: ECs can participate in wholesale and retail markets through PPAs, tenders and standard supplier/aggregator relationships; they are entitled to proportionate, non?discriminatory treatment as final consumers, producers, suppliers and market operators.
column45: Direct wholesale trading by ECs is legally possible but uncommon; most ECs sell via support schemes, PPAs with suppliers or through standard market intermediaries.

column50: Distribution tariffs are set nationally by TSO (CRE); CSC and EC participants face usual capacity and energy?based charges via their suppliers, with no separate EC tariff category.

column54: Formally inclusive but procedurally selective. French REC/CEC law codifies open and voluntary participation, and CSC allows collective sharing through a legal organising entity. In practice, access is mediated by legal, technical, financial and administrative capacity: citizen-energy initiatives are often driven by organised collectives, local authorities, cooperatives, social landlords or other intermediaries, while ordinary low-income households are less likely to initiate projects independently. Evidence from French CRE research points to homogeneous and limited membership bases, suggesting participation is skewed toward actors with higher “participatory capital.” Social-housing CSC schemes exist and may improve access for tenants, but they are often landlord-led; this can deliver distributional benefits while leaving weaker procedural agency for residents
column55: Distributive justice in French EC/CSC schemes is highly design-dependent. The allocation rule determines which participants receive shared production in each settlement interval, while TURPE/network charges, taxes and the price of shared electricity shape the actual bill benefit. The default pro-rata-to-consumption allocation may favour participants with higher contemporaneous consumption unless alternative sharing rules are chosen. Investment-based citizen projects can concentrate benefits among members able to finance or co-own assets, whereas social-housing CSC can extend benefits to tenants but is often landlord-led and may prioritise collective building charges before individual bill reductions. Broader local benefits depend on governance choices, pricing policy and the reinvestment of surpluses.
column59: Overlapping EC, CSC and support?scheme provisions make the framework hard to navigate; there is no published national assessment of REC/CEC obstacles, and some decrees restrict combinations of support mechanisms for citizen projects.
column60: Citizen and local projects compete in tenders dominated by larger commercial players; there is no dedicated route for ECs to monetise flexibility, and tender and PPA complexity can deter smaller initiatives.
column61: CSC and EC operation depend on advanced metering and DSO data processes; complexity grows when participants join multiple CSC operations or ECs and when perimeters approach the 20 km limit.
column62: Small citizen?led projects face financing challenges and are sensitive to changes in support schemes; revised FiP rules and limitations on stacking support mechanisms have reduced their financial attractiveness.
column63: Awareness and organisational capacity are uneven across territories; participation tends to be higher where strong local networks and intermediaries (e.g. Énergie Partagée) are present, raising concerns about the inclusion of less?organised or lower?income communities. Because participants are mostly from homogenous groups, most ECs in France get stuck at small size and don't scale up.

column2: Fully interconnected all?island system (Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland) operated as the Single Electricity Market, with a meshed transmission grid and growing renewable penetration
column3: Fully liberalised wholesale and retail electricity market with unbundled TSOs and competitive suppliers under the Integrated Single Electricity Market (I?SEM) framework (w/ Norther Ireland, and the rest of the EU)
column4: High and rapidly growing renewable share, with onshore wind as the dominant source and renewables providing around 40% of electricity in 2020 and targeted to reach 80% by 2030
column5: CRU (regulator). Transmission operated by EirGrid (Ireland) and SONI (Northern Ireland) as TSOs, with ESB Networks as the main distribution system operator, complemented by interconnectors to Great Britain
column6: 1 138 Sustainable Energy Communities (SECs) registered with SEAI by 2024, with a government ambition to reach 1 500 SECs and at least 10 community renewable electricity projects by 2030
column7: No fully operational, explicitly labelled cVPPs; community projects are mainly generation?oriented with some pilots exploring storage and local trading
column8: Community projects focus on onshore wind farms, rooftop and ground?mounted solar PV, and some small?scale hydro and biomass, increasingly linked to retrofits, efficiency and smart?energy measures
column10: Ireland combines a fully liberalised all?island electricity market with a strong, policy?driven Sustainable Energy Communities programme; SECs act as broad local collaboration platforms, while RECs are defined mainly within support schemes (RESS/SRESS) for small?scale generation, resulting in a large and growing SEC network but relatively few formally defined REC projects so far.
column11: Yes - RECs are defined in the terms and conditions of the Small?Scale Renewable Electricity Support Scheme (SRESS, formerly in RESS) as legal entities based on open and voluntary participation, autonomy and effective local control, whose primary purpose is to provide environmental, economic or social community benefits rather than profit; the definition is scheme?based rather than set in primary energy legislation.
column12: No explicit Citizen Energy Community (CEC) definition exists in Irish energy legislation; the active “community” concepts are Renewable Energy Communities under SRESS/RESS and Sustainable Energy Communities (SECs) under SEAI programmes.
column13: Partial – Ireland has introduced a REC definition in support?scheme terms (RESS/SRESS) and operates a broad Sustainable Energy Communities framework, but has not embedded REC and CEC concepts with full rights and obligations into primary electricity or energy law.
column14: There is no stand?alone legal catalogue of REC/SEC rights and obligations in primary law; instead, RECs gain specific rights through support schemes, such as eligibility for SRESS tariffs and dedicated enabling?framework measures, while SECs mainly access grants, mentoring and toolkits under SEAI programmes.
column15: Yes, but fragmented – Ireland has two complementary frameworks: REC as a support?scheme category in RESS/SRESS, and SEC as a broader, programme?based model supported by SEAI’s Community Enabling Framework, rather than a single, consolidated EC title in energy law.
column16: REC status must be demonstrated to the Minister under SRESS terms (e.g. evidence of local control, non?profit purpose and SEC registration), and community projects must navigate support?scheme applications, grid?connection processes and SEAI programme rules; however, there is no codified EC licensing regime and SEC registration itself does not involve a thorough legal?compliance check.
column18:
Ireland distinguishes between legally defined Renewable Energy Communities and SEAI-supported Sustainable Energy Communities. RECs are formal legal entities derived from EU law, with requirements on open and voluntary participation, autonomy, local/proximity-based control and a primary community-benefit purpose, typically linked to renewable project ownership or development. SECs are broader SEAI network/support structures for local energy planning, efficiency, renewable opportunities and community capacity-building; they are not automatically legal energy communities but can act as a pipeline through which communities develop the capacity, governance and project pipeline needed to become or create RECs.

Ireland’s EC framework is policy? and scheme?driven rather than law?driven: SECs are recognised and supported administratively by SEAI, while RECs exist primarily as a category within RESS/SRESS terms and conditions; there is no national statute that systematically sets out EC rights, obligations or barrier?removal duties comparable to EAG/EIWOG in Austria or the French Energy Code.
column19: REC: any legal entity form that can satisfy SRESS REC criteria (open and voluntary participation, autonomy, democratic governance, non?profit primary purpose); at least one member must be a Sustainable Energy Community registered with SEAI. SEC: does not need to be a separate legal entity, but must have a defined organisational structure and stakeholder commitment as part of SEAI’s SEC programme.
column20: REC members and shareholders may be natural persons, SMEs, local authorities (including municipalities), not?for?profit organisations and local community organisations, provided that participation does not constitute their primary commercial or professional activity (except for SECs); each shareholder or member has one vote regardless of shareholding, and the primary purpose must be community or environmental benefit rather than financial profit.
column21: REC members and controlling stakeholders (natural persons, SMEs, local authorities) must be resident or located in the proximity of the REC project in order to qualify under SRESS; SECs are defined by a geographically bounded community or shared field of interest but are not tied to a specific “proximity” rule in law.
column22: Both REC and SEC frameworks emphasise open and voluntary participation, democratic governance and one?member?one?vote in RECs, with SECs framed as community?led partnerships involving households, clubs, churches, businesses and other local actors working together on energy projects.
column23: Local authorities can be REC members and play roles in SECs, while the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) is the central public actor coordinating SEC registration, grants, mentoring and the Community Enabling Framework; the Department of Environment, Climate and Communications (DECC) designs RESS/SRESS, including REC?specific provisions and community benefit rules.
column24: Commercial developers and suppliers can partner with SECs and RECs, particularly in RESS and SRESS projects and in setting up Community Benefit Funds, but RECs must remain autonomous and effectively controlled by local stakeholders, and third?party involvement must respect one?member?one?vote and non?profit primary purpose conditions.
column26: SECs function as broad local governance platforms for energy efficiency, renewables and smart?energy actions, often preceding concrete generation projects; RECs then emerge as more formalised entities when communities seek to access SRESS tariffs or RESS?related mechanisms, so governance in practice is often a two?step process moving from SEC organising to REC project vehicles.
column27: No - Ireland has an operational microgeneration and export-remuneration framework, including self-consumption, smart-metered export and Clean Export Guarantee payments, and energy sharing/trading is legally recognised for active consumers and energy communities. However, a mature statutory kWh-sharing regime comparable to France’s CSC model is still under regulatory development. Current community-level electricity activity therefore occurs mainly through microgeneration export payments, community-owned generation, supplier/aggregation arrangements such as Community Power, PPAs, grants and contractual/financial benefit-sharing, rather than through a fully implemented regulated energy-sharing allocation mechanism.
column28: Mainly community-owned/co-owned wind and solar generation, RESS/SRESS-linked community benefit funds, and SEC-led energy-efficiency/retrofit planning.
column29: REC definitions require that members (natural persons, SMEs, local authorities) are resident in or located in the “proximity” of the REC project, but there is no grid?level perimeter (e.g. LV/MV) defined in law; SECs operate at community scale (parishes, towns, neighbourhoods or thematic communities) as defined in SEAI’s programme rather than by specific distance constraints.
column30: RECs and SECs do not have a separate supplier?like status; electricity from community projects is typically sold into the market or under support schemes via licensed suppliers or market participants, while local households remain standard customers and receive benefits through tariffs, grants or Community Benefit Fund allocations.
column31: The absence of a tailored legal energy?sharing framework means communities wanting to move beyond generation ownership face uncertainty about local trading, billing and data?sharing; grid?connection processes and market rules are documented in SEAI’s grid?connection toolkit but remain technically and administratively demanding for volunteer?led groups.
column33: Policy emphasis is on community participation in generation and on local benefit distribution (e.g. Community Benefit Funds) rather than on statutory frameworks for sharing kilowatt?hours among members; any “sharing” happens via financial and governance mechanisms rather than meter?level allocation.
column34: National roll?out of smart meters is ongoing, led by ESB Networks, with a focus on enabling active consumers, time?of?use tariffs and greater integration of renewables. Challenges with roll out situation - Cost benefit analysis was considered positive in 2014, then negative. But roll out since has happened - estimated at 0% in 2020 but in sept 2025, ESB Networks announced that it has successfully installed over two million smart meters in homes, farms and businesses across every county in Ireland. More than 4/5 households across the country now have a smart meter installed. (ESB Networks website)
column35: Smart meters provide half-hourly consumption/export data, supporting time-of-use tariffs, dynamic retail pricing, microgeneration export measurement and basic demand-side flexibility. Ireland’s retail and SEM settlement architecture remains largely half-hourly, unlike countries moving to 15-minute energy-sharing/allocation intervals. This is sufficient for supplier-led tariffs and broad aggregation, but less precise for cVPP optimisation, local flexibility settlement and granular intra-community benefit allocation (unless supplemented by aggregator/device-level data).
column38: SEAI’s 2025 impact study on SECs highlights data gaps as a barrier to monitoring and evaluating community impacts and recommends strengthening data infrastructure and reporting for community projects.
column39: Yes - aggregation is allowed under general electricity?market rules, and CRU has developed enabling regulatory frameworks for active consumers and energy communities to participate in markets via suppliers and aggregators.
column40: Independent aggregators can operate in the Irish market under CRU rules, but there is no distinct “community aggregator” legal category; ECs would typically access aggregation services through standard commercial aggregators or suppliers.
column41: In practice, SECs and RECs have so far focused more on project development, grants and support schemes than on providing formal aggregation services, and their potential role in flexibility markets remains largely at the pilot and concept stage.
column43: Policy and regulatory documents increasingly reference “active consumers and energy communities” as future flexibility actors, but concrete pathways for community?led aggregation (e.g. standard products, risk allocation) are still underdeveloped compared with individual and supplier?driven models.
column44: Communities access electricity markets mainly through participation in support schemes (RESS, SRESS) and via standard supplier/market?participant roles for their projects; households and local organisations typically remain regular retail customers.
column45: Community?owned projects can sell electricity into the wholesale market indirectly via suppliers or under RESS/SRESS contracts, with RESS auctions and SRESS fixed tariffs providing structured revenue for eligible community and small?scale projects.
column46: Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (design of RESS/SRESS and ORESS), SEAI (SEC network, Community Enabling Framework, grants), CRU (regulation of active consumers, market rules), EirGrid and ESB Networks (system and network operators) and community organisations and developers participating in auctions and benefit?fund governance.
column48: RESS auctions and SRESS non?competitive tariffs give communities structured routes into the market, but the absence of a statutory EC category and the technical demands of grid?connection and auction participation mean many communities rely heavily on external developers and SEAI mentoring.
column49: There are no EC?specific network?charge reductions; community projects and members face standard network?usage charges set under CRU regulation, with financial advantages mainly delivered via support?scheme tariffs, grants and Community Benefit Funds rather than through differentiated grid fees.
column51: Key schemes include SRESS (non?competitive tariffs for 50 kW–6 MW projects from communities, farmers and SMEs, with 15?year support and technology?specific tariffs), SEAI’s Community Energy Grant (for efficiency and retrofit projects), and RESS/ORESS Community Benefit Funds, which require developers to contribute around EUR 2/MWh and allocate at least 40% of funds to community?oriented SDG projects, with minimum payments to near neighbours in onshore wind auctions.
column54: SECs provide an accessible entry point for community?led energy projects and are supported by SEAI mentoring and toolkits, but there is no statutory EC rights framework; complex support?scheme and grid?connection procedures mean that effective participation still depends heavily on capacity, external support and engagement with developers.
column55: Community Benefit Funds aim to channel financial benefits to local communities (including near?neighbour payments and SDG?aligned projects), but impact studies show unequal uptake, with more advantaged communities more likely to mobilise and access grants and funds.
column59: Lack of a comprehensive legal definition of EC rights and obligations, absence of a CEC category and reliance on scheme?based REC definitions create legal uncertainty for communities wishing to move beyond support?scheme participation into broader market roles.
column60: Participation in RESS auctions and in SRESS, as well as negotiating grid connections and power?purchase arrangements, can be challenging for volunteer?led communities, leading to dependence on commercial partners and raising concerns about communities’ bargaining power and long?term value capture.
column61: Limited in?house technical expertise on grid connection, metering, project design and monitoring within many communities slows project development and increases reliance on external consultants and developers.
column62: Dependance on short funding cycles; high upfront development costs and the need to pre?finance studies and applications can be prohibitive for smaller or less affluent communities, even when long?term tariffs or grants are available.
column63: SEAI’s 2025 impact study finds under?representation of lower?income communities and notes that participation is strongest where social capital and local organisational capacity are already high, raising concerns about an unequal distribution of opportunities and benefits.
column64: Data gaps and limited monitoring of community?level outcomes make it difficult to assess and communicate the full impact of SECs and REC?type projects, which in turn can hinder policy learning and public trust.
column65: A large and expanding SEC network, SRESS tariffs tailored to community and small?scale projects, and RESS/ORESS Community Benefit Funds offer strong levers to grow community energy; targeted reforms to strengthen legal recognition, stabilise funding, enhance technical support and prioritise lower?income communities could turn Ireland’s scheme?driven model into a more robust, justice?oriented EC framework.

column2: Hydro?dominated, partially centralised electricity system with significant nuclear baseload, large pumped?hydro storage and a growing share of decentralised solar PV
column3: Wholesale market liberalised and integrated with neighbouring countries; retail market still only partially liberalised, with many consumers supplied by vertically integrated municipal and regional utilities that remain dominant in their service areas (semi-private system of electricity providers where each county (canton) or city in Switzerland has its own power distributor, with private companies competing to supply them with electricity.
column4: High renewable share dominated by large hydro (run?of?river and storage) and pumped?hydro storage, with rapidly growing rooftop and ground?mounted solar PV and a smaller contribution from wind and biomass
column5: Swissgrid operates the national TSO ; distribution is handled by a fragmented landscape of municipal and regional DSOs, many of them vertically integrated utilities that combine supply and distribution; local grids play a key role in hosting decentralised PV and emerging self?consumption and local electricity community schemes
column6: No unified national count, but several hundred associations for self?consumption (ZEV) and similar self?consumption clusters are reported by utilities and research projects, with numbers growing quickly since their introduction in 2018 (various utility and research sources rather than a single official registry)
column7: No explicitly labelled community virtual power plants
column8: Energy communities mainly develop rooftop and building?integrated PV in multi?apartment buildings and neighbourhoods, often combined with behind?the?meter batteries, heat pumps and smart?control solutions; some local energy communities also coordinate with or integrate small hydro and exploit the flexibility of Swiss hydro and storage at higher grid levels
column10: Switzerland’s EC landscape is built around “associations for self?consumption” (ZEV) and emerging local electricity communities, which enable shared use of local PV
column11: No – Switzerland is not bound by RED II and has no “renewable energy community (REC)” definition; instead, energy?community?like constructs are defined as self?consumption associations (ZEV) and, more recently, local electricity communities (LEGs) in national energy legislation and ordinances
column12: No – no explicit “citizen energy community (CEC)” category; Swiss law uses technology? and source?neutral constructs (ZEV and LEG) that play a similar functional role but are not labelled as CECs
column13: Not applicable / Not transposed – Switzerland is outside the EU. Instead, Switzerland has built its own national framework, now centred on ZEV/vZEV and especially LEG as of 2026
column14: Under the updated framework, Swiss energy communities may generate, consume, store and locally share renewable electricity; LEG participants can trade/share electricity over the public distribution grid under defined proximity and metering conditions, while ZEV/vZEV arrangements organise collective self-consumption more as a single end-customer structure. They do not generally own public electricity networks, but they can organise internal allocation, billing and optimisation, and they may interact with suppliers, DSOs and digital service providers for settlement and flexibility-related services
column15: Yes – Switzerland has a dedicated framework for collective/local energy communities through ZEV, vZEV and, most importantly in 2026, LEG, mainly under the Electricity Supply Act (StromVG) and Electricity Supply Ordinance (StromVV), alongside the earlier self-consumption framework
column16: there is no REC/CEC registry as such, but LEGs require formal setup with the supplier/DSO, smart metering, compliance with proximity/grid-level rules and adapted billing/data processes; this makes LEG more operationally complex than a simple behind-the-meter ZEV
column18: For Switzerland, LEG should now be treated as the leading and most up-to-date EC-type structure, because it expands community electricity sharing beyond the classic ZEV model and does so through the public grid under regulated tariff reductions
column19: No specific framework prescribed - ZEV, vZEV and LEG can use standard Swiss legalforms such as associations, cooperatives, limited liability companies (GmbH/Sàrl), public limited companies (AG/SA) or contractual associations under private law
column20:
Members/participants can be citizens, building owners, housing companies, SMEs and municipalities; there is no EC?specific EU?style non?profit or dividend cap, so profit orientation depends on the chosen legal form (e.g. cooperative vs AG/GmbH) and internal statutes.
For LEGs, each consumption site and producer/storage unit can only participate in one LEG, which limits concentration of control at asset/site level (even though no explicit shareholding cap is defined in the LEG provisions as it is is most REC equivalent regulation)
column21:
LEGs must stay local: all participants must be in the same DSO grid area, on the same low?voltage grid level.
ZEV and vZEV are bound to building level (one grid connection).
column22: Citizens can join as individual household members or via housing cooperatives and similar entities, with membership and voting arrangements governed by the underlying legal form (e.g. one?member?one?vote in co?ops, share?based voting in companies, or member assemblies in associations)
column23: Municipalities and municipal utilities are central governance actors: they own grid infrastructure and roofs, initiate many ZEV/vZEV/LEG schemes, and may control the project entity or co?govern it with private actors
column24: Commercial suppliers, DSOs and service providers (utilities, ESCOs, billing/IT platforms) play a strong operational and sometimes strategic role: they design standardised ZEV/vZEV/LEG offers, handle metering, settlement and customer interfaces, and may own or co?own PV assets, which means governance is frequently orchestrated by incumbent energy actors rather than purely citizen?run
column26: Swiss EC?type governance is characterised by hybrid, negotiated arrangements often landlord? or utility?led local schemes with citizen participation rather than a single dominant citizen?majority co?op template
column27: Yes – via collective self?consumption schemes (ZEV and vZEV) where a self?consumption consortium allocates shared PV production among members, and via LEG, which allows participants to sell and share electricity with each other over the public distribution grid at reduced network tariffs within a defined local area
column28: Combination of collective self?consumption (ZEV/vZEV) of local PV with internal allocation and billing, and a LEG model in which individually metered consumers, producers and storage units have their own contracts with suppliers but engage in local energy sharing and trading over the public grid under a regulated local?tariff framework
column29: ZEV is confined to one grid connection and private lines across one or several physically connected buildings; vZEV uses the DSO’s low?voltage lines to connect participants at the production site; LEG must be within the same DSO grid area and low?voltage level
column30: In ZEV/vZEV, the consortium is treated as a single final customer behind a main meter, with an external supplier serving the ZEV and the ZEV operator allocating and billing internally; in LEG, all participants keep their individual supply contracts and market access, while the DSO provides the grid for intra?LEG exchanges at a discounted network tariff and suppliers handle residual supply and settlement
column31: configurations must be set up and validated with the DSO and supplier, making implementation administratively and technically demanding
column34: Medium to high and rapidly progressing but no specific figure found – DSOs are legally required to replace at least 80% of conventional meters with remotely readable smart meters by the end of 2027 (Energy Act / StromVV), and several utilities aim for near?100% coverage by around 2028; smart meters are effectively mandatory for participants in ZEV, vZEV and LEG schemes
column35: 15?minute metering is the typical standard for mass?deployed smart meters in Switzerland, aligned with European practice and used for billing, settlement and flexibility applications
column36:
Distribution network operators own and operate the metering infrastructure, collect 15?minute data and provide it to suppliers for billing and settlement; customers can access their own consumption data via utility portals (e.g. “My ewz”) and, with consent, share it with third?party service providers, in line with Swiss/EU?inspired data?protection and consumer?empowerment principles.

Energy communities (ZEV/vZEV/LEG) typically receive aggregated allocation and billing data via their supplier/DSO interfaces rather than full raw meter streams; detailed EC?level data feeds and standardised interfaces are still emerging, and the exact role/allocation model can vary by DSO and supplier.
column38: Key barriers include the need to complete both the physical rollout (reaching the 80% mandate and, in some cases, replacing early smart meters) and the development of harmonised, consumer?friendly data?access frameworks for ECs; without consistent 15?minute data access and clear substitute?value procedures, more advanced LEG and flexibility use cases remain administratively and technically challenging.
column39: Yes – aggregation of distributed generation and demand?side flexibility is allowed; aggregators can pool distributed resources (generation units, loads, storage) to provide balancing reserves (aFRR/mFRR) and other ancillary and flexibility services.
column40: Independent aggregators are effectively recognised through a “central settlement” model: Swissgrid’s ancillary?services framework allows an aggregator/reserve provider to pool technical units from different balance?responsible groups, with Swissgrid performing central settlement of activated energy so that BRPs are compensated; this enables aggregator participation without full supplier/BRP integration, though regulatory and contractual details still matter
column41:
There is no explicit “community aggregator” licence or EC?specific aggregation category, but energy?community?type entities (ZEVs, LEGs, local utilities acting on their behalf) can, in principle, provide flexibility via aggregators or act as aggregators themselves under general ancillary?service and flexibility?market rules, provided they or their partners meet Swissgrid’s technical, metering and telemetry requirements.

Several Swiss projects and utilities already aggregate geographically distributed resources (including prosumers) for reserve provision and local flexibility, indicating that community?level aggregation is technically and institutionally feasible even if not framed as a distinct legal category.
column43: Interaction with Swissgrid and DSOs is structured via the central?settlement balancing model and emerging local flexibility/tariff schemes: aggregators remain responsible to Swissgrid for reserve delivery, while DSOs explore tariff? and market?based ways to harness local flexibility from prosumers and ECs; regulatory discussions focus on avoiding conflicts with BRPs and ensuring fair compensation and transparent responsibilities for all parties
column44: EC?type actors (ZEVs, LEGs and similar local schemes) can sell electricity via suppliers and PPAs, participate indirectly in wholesale and balancing markets through BRPs and aggregators, and provide flexibility in emerging TSO–DSO coordination and local flexibility schemes; they have no dedicated “EC market” but operate under general market rules for prosumers and aggregators
column45: Direct wholesale trading is legally possible for entities that assume balance?responsible roles, but in practice EC?type projects rely on utilities, suppliers or aggregators to handle wholesale and balancing?market participation, with communities typically focusing on local generation, self?consumption and flexibility provision rather than direct exchange trading.
column46: Key actors for EC market access are the federal regulator and energy ministry (setting framework conditions), the TSO Swissgrid (responsible for procuring ancillary services and running balancing markets), a fragmented set of DSOs and municipal utilities (critical for local flexibility, ZEV/LEG implementation and grid?tariff schemes), and research/innovation projects (e.g. Equigy crowd?balancing, Swissgrid–ewz pilots, joint TSO–DSO flexibility?market initiatives) that define how decentralised resources, including ECs, can participate
column48: Swiss law and regulatory strategy emphasise non?discriminatory access to markets and the integration of decentralised flexibility via central?settlement balancing models and coordinated TSO–DSO schemes; however, there is no explicit priority access or EC?specific market rule, and EC participation depends on meeting general technical requirements and on arrangements with BRPs, aggregators and DSOs.
column49: ZEV/vZEV self?consumption behind a common connection point avoids volumetric grid charges on the self?consumed portion (treated as behind?the?meter), but any electricity taken from or injected into the public grid pays standard network tariffs; in contrast, LEG internal exchanges over the public grid benefit from a legally defined reduction in network usage tariffs (up to 60%, currently set at 40% or 20% depending on grid levels involved)
column50: Swiss grid tariffs for end?users combine energy?based and power?based components, differentiated by grid level and connection size; recent reforms restructure transmission?grid usage into working and power tariffs and introduce a small solidarity surcharge, while at distribution level operators are beginning to offer dynamic and location?differentiated tariffs and to apply reduced network usage tariffs for LEG internal flows in line with StromVV (40% or 20% discounts)
column51: General Swiss RES support (investment grants and feed?in remuneration for PV and other renewables) is accessible to ZEV/LEG projects, but there are no EC?specific subsidies; Swiss ECs are not eligible for core EU EC funding schemes such as the EECF and mostly rely on national, cantonal and utility programmes.
column53:
Because network?tariff reductions are significant only for LEG internal exchanges (and ZEV gains mainly come from avoiding retail energy and grid charges on behind?the?meter consumption), Swiss EC viability hinges on high self?consumption ratios, the new LEG grid?tariff discounts, and general PV subsidies.
Rising grid?usage costs and tariff reforms can erode savings if communities export large shares or fail to optimise consumption and flexibility, reinforcing the importance of storage, demand shifting and careful tariff/technology design.
column59:
Complex, fragmented legal framework (EnG, EnV, StromVG, StromVV) with detailed eligibility, proximity and membership rules for ZEV/vZEV/LEG, making EC design legally demanding for non?experts.

Hard proximity and exclusivity constraints (one consumption site per LEG, one LEG per site, single municipal area) limit scaling across municipalities and make it harder to optimise larger regional portfolios
column60:
ECs must integrate into existing supplier/BRP arrangements, with no dedicated EC market regime; complex billing and settlement rules for LEG (including discounted grid tariffs and centralised allocation) raise transaction costs and discourage some suppliers from actively supporting EC products.

Tariff and market incentives can favour maximising self?consumption within individual communities over exporting or coordinating with wider system needs, potentially misaligning EC operation with national RES and flexibility objectives
column61:
Smart?meter rollout and ICT requirements (15?minute metering, advanced billing systems) are essential for LEG and vZEV, but not yet fully implemented and standardised across all DSOs, making some advanced configurations difficult in practice.

Complex metering and billing configurations for multi?actor LEGs (different grid levels, mixed producers/consumers, reduced tariffs) increase implementation risk and require high technical competence from DSOs, suppliers and EC organisers
column62:
EC projects (especially LEG) typically require significant up?front investment in PV, storage and control systems, while federal support schemes are generic, competitive and not specifically tailored to ECs, making it harder for smaller citizen initiatives to compete with professional developers.

Current tariff and support structures risk prioritising self?consumption and cost savings for participants over maximising overall renewable output and flexibility, and may not provide sufficient revenue streams to support long?term operation and professional management of ECs.
column63:
LEC/LEG uptake depends on motivated local actors (municipalities, utilities, citizen groups); academic work notes that rural and smaller municipalities often have limited administrative capacity and rely heavily on a few individuals, which can slow or stall initiatives.

Participation may be skewed towards more engaged or better?off citizens, while renters, low?income households and less organised communities risk being left out unless specific inclusion strategies are pursued.
column64:
Siting and spatial planning constraints (landscape protection, noise, local opposition to wind/PV) can limit the development of larger generation assets that would underpin LEGs, especially in rural or alpine municipalities.

Topographical and municipal boundaries interact awkwardly with LEG’s “one municipality” rule, so some geographically coherent areas are split across municipalities and cannot form a single LEG even when technically and socially logical
column65:
LEG introduces, for the first time, a clear, legally defined Swiss local electricity community framework with discounted grid tariffs for internal exchanges, opening a structured pathway for EC?type schemes to scale beyond building?level ZEVs; academic assessments suggest that rural LECs alone could contribute up to roughly a quarter of new renewable?electricity targets if economic conditions (tariffs, feed?in, prices) are tuned appropriately.

Ongoing digitalisation (smart?meter rollout), TSO–DSO flexibility pilots and national decarbonisation targets create a strong policy rationale to integrate ZEV/LEG communities into broader flexibility and system?service markets, providing a potential second value stream (beyond self?consumption savings) that could make Swiss ECs more robust and socially impactful over time

column2: Largely centralised, gas? and wind/solar?dominated mix with significant offshore and onshore wind, strong growth in solar PV and a legacy of gas?fired generation and some nuclear
column3: Fully liberalised wholesale and retail markets with competitive suppliers and trading; legacy incumbents and large energy companies still hold significant market shares, but entry barriers are relatively low as Dutch law regulates activities rather than specific player types
column4: High and fast?growing renewable share, driven primarily by offshore and onshore wind and rapidly expanding solar PV, with bioenergy as an important additional renewable source and only minor contributions from hydro and geothermal.
column5: TenneT operates the national transmission system as the unbundled TSO, while a small number of regional DSOs (e.g. Enexis, Liander, Stedin and a few smaller operators) own and run the distribution networks; the system faces widespread grid?congestion issues due to rapid electrification and decentralised generation, prompting major grid?reinforcement and congestion?management programmes.
column6: ?700–1,400 citizen energy initiatives and energy cooperatives (2023–2024, NECP and national mapping studies), with 714 energy cooperatives reported in the updated NECP and at least 700 broader citizen initiatives, many of which are expected to qualify as “energy community” legal entities under the new Energy Act. Among the largest average number of members of EC in Europe
column7: Pilots only – several local energy communities and smart?grid projects (e.g. Endona, Energie Coöperatie Loenen and other sandbox/SmartCORE pilots) test aggregation, flexibility and community supply models, but there is no systematic national category of explicitly labelled community virtual power plants.
column8: Dutch energy communities mainly develop solar PV (especially on rooftops and small solar farms) and onshore wind projects, often supported by the SCE cooperative subsidy scheme; some initiatives also integrate batteries, demand response and other flexible assets in response to grid congestion and local balancing needs

column11: Yes – REC provisions from RED II are consolidated into a unified “energy community” definition in the new Energy Act (primary law, Article 1 and Article 2.4), which treats energy communities as official market participants with a primary non?profit purpose.
column12: Yes – CEC provisions from the Electricity Market Directive are likewise integrated into the same unified “energy community” definition in the Energy Act, so there is no separate CEC category; both REC and CEC concepts are transposed via this single EC legal entity.
column13: Complete – REC/CEC provisions from RED II and the Electricity Market Directive have been transposed into the Energy Act adopted in December 2024 and entering into force from 1 January 2026, with energy communities defined, granted rights and protected against discrimination; some secondary instruments (e.g. ministerial regulation on maximum number of members for supply?licence exemptions) are still pending but do not affect the core transposition
column14:
Energy communities may collectively generate, store, share and supply energy to their members at cost price, and may engage in self?consumption, sale and supply to third parties, and flexibility and energy?efficiency activities, subject to the general market rules and specific EC exemptions laid down in the Energy Act.

They can share energy internally (energy sharing as a distinct legal concept from supply) when members have appropriate contracts and smart metering, and they may supply electricity or gas without a full supplier permit within defined quantitative and membership limits, but they cannot own public transmission or distribution networks and remain subject to unbundling rules
column15: Yes – there is a dedicated EC framework in the new Energy Act (Energiewet), which codifies energy communities as a specific legal entity with open and voluntary participation, local/non?profit purpose and governance requirements, and is complemented by existing Electricity and Gas Acts and implementing regulations for details such as permits, energy sharing and supplier exemptions and allows ECs to takeover any role from the grid.
column16: There is no separate national registry of energy communities yet; ECs must adopt or adapt a legal form under general company/association law, include specific EC clauses in their statutes or partnership agreements to meet Energy Act conditions, and then comply with standard licensing, permitting and DSO/supplier notification procedures. Existence of a regulative exemption where ECs stay within the Energy Act’s thresholds
column19: Cooperatives, associations, foundations and companies (e.g. BV) as well as other standard Dutch legal entities; the Energy Act defines “energy community” as a functional/legal category and allows it to be realised through various underlying legal forms, with cooperatives explicitly recognised as one option.
column20:
Members, partners or shareholders can be natural persons, micro? and small enterprises, municipalities, water authorities, provinces and joint arrangements; for renewable?project ECs, membership can additionally include medium?sized enterprises under specified conditions.
The primary purpose of an energy community must be to deliver environmental, economic or social benefits to members or the local area and “not be aimed at making a profit”, so ECs are formally non?profit in purpose, with detailed shareholding caps not set in the Act but effective control required to remain with the specified local/citizen categories.
column21: For ECs developing renewable projects, actual control must be exercised by members, partners or shareholders that are “established in the vicinity of the renewable energy projects”, creating a de facto local?proximity requirement for controlling members, even though membership in general can be broader.
column22:
Participation in an energy community must be open and voluntary, and members/partners/shareholders must have the right to leave; actual control must rest with natural persons, small/micro enterprises and local public entities (municipalities, provinces, water authorities, joint arrangements), and EC statutes can require equal voting rights among participating members.
In practice, most Dutch ECs are citizen energy cooperatives where individuals join as members with voting rights (typically one?member?one?vote), often alongside local authorities and small businesses, and the Energy Act largely formalises this cooperative?style control model.
column23: Municipalities, provinces and water authorities may be members, partners or shareholders and can hold actual control positions; the climate agreement and national policy encourage local public actors to support and co?own projects, with a political ambition of 50% local ownership of renewable production in many areas
column24: Commercial RES developers, suppliers and service providers (including large utilities and project developers) may partner with or co?own projects alongside energy communities, and crowdfunding platforms and social?impact investors frequently provide capital, but the Energy Act’s governance rules ensure that effective control remains with citizens, local SMEs and public actors rather than with large commercial players.

column26: Citizen?majority energy cooperatives remain the dominant governance archetype, now reclassified as “energy communities” under the Energy Act; many ECs are mixed vehicles combining citizen co?ops, municipalities and professional developers, but with legal requirements that local/non?profit stakeholders retain effective control
column27: Yes – via a legally defined “energy sharing” mechanism (distinct from supply) where active consumers within an energy community exchange self?generated electricity with each other in real time, subject to conditions in the Energy Act (Article 2.30) and implemented through participating suppliers
column28: Supplier?mediated energy sharing of locally generated electricity within an energy community, combined with collective generation/self?consumption and residual supply from commercial suppliers at cost?price for members
column29: The Act allows rules to be set on the location where energy may be shared (e.g. defining the spatial scope of the community), and sharing must occur within the defined energy community perimeter so that generation and consumption are located “within that community”, with exchanges settled per imbalance settlement period.
column30: Participants must all have a contract with an energy supplier that offers energy?sharing services, and all members with whom energy is shared must also have a supply or return contract with that same supplier; the supplier mediates and settles shared energy while continuing to provide standard supply for residual volumes. The Energy Act creates a rule that prevents a market participant fromdisadvantaging or preventing a final or active customer from participating in an energycommunity. Provisions in agreements between market actors and final or active customersthat contravene this rule are voidable
column31:
Energy sharing is only possible under the Energy Act’s defined conditions: EC members must use a supplier that supports energy sharing, all members must have smart meters with communication functionality activated, and electricity must be shared per imbalance settlement period, with additional limits and rules applicable to ECs using supply?licence exemptions (e.g. annual balance between supply and feed?in, small?connection end users, and a maximum number of members to be fixed by ministerial regulation).
These metering, supplier?alignment and quantitative constraints, plus the absence (so far) of detailed implementing rules on member caps, create practical bottlenecks and uncertainty for scaling energy?sharing schemes beyond early adopters and cooperative–supplier partnerships
