column33: The law leaves room for different internal allocation rules (e.g. pro?rata to consumption, fixed shares), but in practice Dutch ECs are likely to start with relatively simple sharing rules that suppliers and metering systems can handle, and energy sharing is at an early stage as the Energy Act only enters into force from 2026. Suppliers are still developing products and legislators are still developping additional conditions that would allow scale ups.
column34: High (82.5% in 2020) but not yet fully complete – most households already have smart meters, and the new Energy Act requires remaining analogue meters to be replaced by 2030; at the same time, around 2.5 million first?generation GPRS smart meters must be swapped out before 2G networks shut down in 2029, with modular replacements rolling out from 2027
column35: 15?minute data aligned with the EU?wide 15?minute imbalance settlement and market time unit, which is the minimum granularity needed for energy sharing to be settled per imbalance period
column36:
DSOs collect metering data and provide it to suppliers for billing and settlement; under the new Energy Act and related data?sharing rules, suppliers and grid operators must use this data to implement energy?sharing allocations, while consumers gain stronger rights to access their own consumption/production data and share it with third?party services in a GDPR?compliant way.

Energy communities as legal entities receive allocation/settlement information indirectly via their partner suppliers/DSOs and can use it for internal allocation, reporting and member billing, while individual members access their own data through supplier/DSO portals and APIs; direct, standardised EC?level data feeds are emerging but not yet fully harmonised.

column38: Key bottlenecks include the dual task of replacing both remaining analogue meters and a large stock of obsolete first?generation smart meters, ensuring that all devices support 15?minute data and remote communication; until this is resolved, some ECs and suppliers may face constraints in rolling out energy?sharing products nationwide and in integrating high?frequency data into their billing and allocation systems
column39: Yes – aggregation of generation and demand?side flexibility is allowed; aggregators can pool distributed resources (PV, batteries, flexible loads) for wholesale, balancing and flexibility services, and energy communities are explicitly allowed to be active in flexibility and energy?efficiency fields under the Energy Act.
column40: Independent aggregators (separate from suppliers) are recognised in Dutch law as part of the transposition of the Electricity Market Directive; they can provide demand?response and other flexibility services, but their market access often requires contractual arrangements and compensation mechanisms with suppliers and BRPs, and detailed secondary rules are still evolving
column41:
Energy communities are not given a distinct “community aggregator” licence, but the Energy Act allows them to engage in flexibility and energy?efficiency activities and to contract for or provide flexibility services; in practice, Dutch energy cooperatives (through their federation Energie Samen and projects like FLEXCoop) can already aggregate member loads to participate in TSO balancing reserves and other flexibility products (as is the case with the coop Endona)

This means ECs can either act as aggregators themselves under general aggregation rules (if they meet technical and market requirements) or partner with independent/utility aggregators to monetise community flexibility.

column43: Key issues for EC aggregation in the Netherlands include the need to coordinate with DSOs and TSOs on congestion management and balancing, to comply with evolving compensation rules between aggregators and suppliers/BRPs, and to integrate 15?minute smart?meter data and digital platforms; several Dutch case studies highlight both the potential value of community?based flexibility and the regulatory/market complexity of bringing EC aggregation to scale
column44: Energy communities can sell electricity via PPAs with suppliers, participate in wholesale and balancing markets indirectly through BRPs and aggregators, and increasingly provide flexibility for congestion management in DSO and TSO schemes; they also benefit from national support schemes (e.g. SCE) for cooperative generation, but there is no dedicated EC?only local flexibility market yet.
column45: Direct wholesale trading is legally possible in principle if an EC takes on BRP responsibilities, but in practice ECs almost always rely on PPAs and contractual arrangements with suppliers and/or BRPs, who handle day?ahead/intraday trading and balancing on their behalf
column46: Key actors for EC market access are the national regulator (ACM), the TSO TenneT, regional DSOs (e.g. Liander, Enexis, Stedin) running congestion and flexibility pilots, and national and EU?level community?support organisations and projects (e.g. Energie Samen, REScoop projects, cVPP and related research programmes) that help ECs navigate markets and aggregation.

column48: The Energy Act includes non?discrimination and “no blocking” clauses (e.g. suppliers and other market participants may not prevent customers from joining ECs or engaging in self?consumption, energy sharing, flexibility or energy?efficiency activities), and EU rules guarantee consumers’ right to access all electricity markets; however, the technical and contractual complexity of BRP responsibilities, aggregation and flexibility procurement still limits ECs’ effective participation to a subset of more advanced, often pilot?based initiatives
column49: Shared and self?consumed energy generally pays standard volumetric and/or capacity?based grid tariffs, with only minimal tariff adaptations for shared electricity over 15?minute periods within buildings approved so far; there is no broad EC?specific reduction in network charges for energy shared via the new energy?sharing mechanism
column50: DSO tariffs are set nationally and remain mostly capacity? and energy?based, differentiated by connection size and voltage level, with emerging discussion of dynamic grid tariffs that reflect local congestion and could, in future, better reward local flexibility; currently, however, tariff structures provide only weak price signals or incentives specifically tailored to energy?community flows
column51:
The key EC?relevant support scheme is the Subsidy Scheme for Cooperative Energy Generation (SCE), an operating per?kWh subsidy for renewable electricity projects (mainly solar PV, onshore wind and small hydro) developed and owned by energy cooperatives and Owners’ Associations within the same postcode area.
More generally, Dutch community projects can also access broader RES schemes like SDE/SDE++ (operating grants for renewable generation) and new cooperative financing instruments such as the Energie Samen development funds, but these are not reserved exclusively for ECs, and access often depends on project size and professionalisation

column59:
Energy?sharing and EC supply?licence exemptions still depend on secondary rules (e.g. maximum number of members, detailed implementation by suppliers/ACM), creating uncertainty for EC planning.
Existing support and EC rules focus mainly on electricity and specific legal forms (co?ops, VvEs), making it harder to extend EC models to multi?vector projects (heat, mobility) or other entity types.
column60:
Market design remains complex for small actors: ECs usually must work through suppliers, BRPs and aggregators to access wholesale, balancing and flexibility markets, with limited transparency and transaction costs that deter smaller communities.
There is no dedicated, stable local flexibility market design yet; pilots exist, but long?term procurement frameworks for community flexibility are still evolving
column61:
Severe grid congestion and limited connection capacity in many regions delay or cap new EC generation and make project development contingent on DSO reinforcement or congestion?management schemes.
Smart?meter rollout is high but not complete, and first?generation meters need replacement; implementing supplier?mediated energy sharing with 15?minute metering and complex multi?member allocation is technically demanding for both ECs and suppliers
column62:
Small cooperative projects face difficulties securing finance and managing risk in a volatile price environment, especially as support schemes (SCE/SDE++) are competitive, time?limited and may favour better?resourced developers.
Standard grid tariffs and price structures provide limited financial reward for local self?consumption and energy sharing, so EC business cases often hinge on subsidies rather than on underlying tariff signals.
column63:
Energy?community participation is uneven: academic case studies highlight that projects often draw on higher?income, more educated citizens, while low?income households and renters are under?represented and face barriers such as limited capital, information and time.
Volunteer fatigue and governance capacity issues within co?ops (e.g. reliance on a small core of active members) limit their ability to scale up, professionalise and engage with complex market and regulatory arrangements.
column64:
Spatial planning and siting conflicts (e.g. opposition to wind turbines, competing land uses) constrain large onshore projects, even where local co?ownership is offered, and environmental rules can slow down permitting for both wind and solar.

Municipal governance and administrative capacity vary widely, so some municipalities strongly support ECs while others are cautious or slow, leading to very uneven enabling conditions across the country
column65:
The new Energy Act gives ECs a formal, non?profit legal status, explicit rights to generate, share and (within limits) supply energy, and non?discrimination guarantees, while national schemes such as SCE and broader SDE++ support, plus strong cooperative federations (e.g. Energie Samen) and EU programmes (EECF, NRG2peers, SmartCORE), provide an evolving enabling ecosystem for EC expansion and professionalisation.

At the same time, grid?congestion and flexibility challenges create a structural opportunity for ECs to be recognised as providers of local flexibility and system services, with ongoing pilots and research demonstrating how community?based flexibility and aggregation can support DSOs and TSOs, potentially leading to more systematic flexibility markets and value streams for ECs in the medium term.
